title: Weighted projective planes P(a,b,c) and Egyptian conditions for Fano/Kähler–Einstein
connection: Well-formedness and Fano conditions for P(a,b,c) and for hypersurfaces in weighted projective space are linear/Egyptian conditions on weights (e.g. Σ w_i > d for Fano hypersurfaces). Reid's 95 K3 families arise from such equations.
why: Classification lists of weighted hypersurfaces are generated by Egyptian-type inequalities; an equality version '1/a + 1/b + 1/c = 4/n' may describe a specific family (e.g. degree conditions), giving a geometric home for ES triples.
first_step: Look for weighted hypersurface conditions of the form Σ 1/w_i = r (equality) in Reid's/Iano-Fletcher's lists; match with 4/n.

title: Elliptic-curve ES: '4/P = Σ 1/X_i' in the group law sense (point division) — category check
connection: Unit fractions don't exist in an abelian group of points; replacing 1/x by 'x-coordinate of a point' gives a different problem (sums of x-coordinates). Recorded as a nonsense-adjacent world; only the coordinate-ring version (genus-1 FF world) is meaningful.
why: Prunes a tempting but meaningless analogy.
first_step: None (closed).

title: Galois-cohomology world: ES solutions as rational points of a torsor under a torus
connection: The plane X + Y + Z = 4/n in reciprocal coordinates intersects the 'integrality' conditions; integrality of 1/X is a multiplicative condition, so the integral points are points of a torsor under a split torus (G_m³) restricted to a plane — a log-Calabi–Yau setting.
why: Log-CY integral points have a growing theory (Gross–Hacking–Keel mirror symmetry, cluster varieties); ES might be a cluster-type variety whose integral points have canonical bases.
first_step: Check whether the ES surface (or its log-CY compactification) is a cluster variety; compute its boundary divisor and log-canonical class.

title: ES over Z[√2] with cone 'conjugate ≥ 1' (all embeddings ≥ 1): units excluded, lottery restored?
connection: Elements with all conjugates ≥ 1 form a multiplicatively closed set bounded below by 1 at both places (though dense in [1, ∞) in each embedding) and excluding all non-trivial units. This 'height-positive' cone should behave like ℕ (hard).
why: If computations show ES over this cone fails for some rational p, it is a hard world with richer arithmetic; if it always holds, there is a mechanism beyond units worth extracting.
first_step: Search 4/p = Σ 1/x_i with x_i ∈ Z[√2], x_i, x_i' ≥ 1, for p ≤ 2000, bounded height; compare with integer solution counts.

title: Effective Hilbert-irreducibility world: ES-good p as values outside thin sets of a parameter family
connection: Each Type II family is a rational map from parameters to p; p is ES-good iff it is a value of some family. 'Values of a polynomial map in all primes' is Hilbert-irreducibility territory (value sets of covers). ES ⇔ the union of value sets of countably many covers contains all p ≡ 1 mod 4.
why: Value-set theorems for covers (e.g. Müller, Dèbes) might give density statements with better error terms than sieve methods.
first_step: Formalize Type II families as covers P¹ ← C and look up value-set results for families of covers of growing degree.

title: Feature: height growth / Baker-type forcing
connection: Dividing-line feature 'height growth / Baker-type forcing'. ES LACKS (no linear forms in logarithms appear). To supply it one could: seek a formulation where nonexistence of an ES certificate forces a very good rational approximation or a small linear form in logs, contradicting Baker
why: Primitive divisors (BHV), Catalan-type results use Baker-type lower bounds to force existence of divisors.
first_step: Ask: if every 4Cp+1 (C ≤ X) has all prime factors in a subgroup H_C avoiding −1, is there an associated multiplicative relation among small primes that Baker could forbid?

title: Transfer: Legendre negative-Pell descent ported to ES
connection: Legendre: from x² − py² = 1 (x odd) factor (x−1)(x+1) = py² and case-split to obtain x² − py² = −1. For ES: start from a forced identity involving p (e.g. a Pell solution, or p = a² + b²) and case-split its factors into ES certificates.
why: Uses the only known O(1)-count pointwise mechanism at p ≡ 1 mod 4 that is purely elementary.
first_step: Take p = a² + b² (Fermat, forced) and test whether (a,b) give ES certificates via simple formulas for a positive fraction of p; record failures.

title: Feature: hereditary consistency across scales (ES(p) solutions at p shape solutions at p·k)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'hereditary consistency across scales (ES(p) solutions at p shape solutions at p·k)'. ES HAS trivial scaling. To supply it one could: seek non-trivial 'lifting' from n = pq to p, i.e. a solution for 4/(pq) which is not a scaled 4/p solution, giving info about p
why: Non-trivial composite information might feed back to primes via descent.
first_step: Count non-scaled solutions of 4/(pq) and test whether their existence correlates with R(p).

title: U(p) uncorrelated with a_p of non-CM elliptic curves
connection: Spearman of U(p)-residual with a_p(11a1)/2√p is +0.004, with a_p(37a1)/2√p −0.005, with |a_p(32a1)|/2√p +0.007, with Ramanujan τ(p)/p^{5.5} +0.006 (n≈9 000).
why: Null result: no detectable dependence on these Hecke eigenvalues, so a naive 'ES count tracks a fixed non-CM form' fingerprint is not supported; the detected dependence is through quadratic characters/L-values.
first_step: Repeat with weight-2 newforms of level 4·d for d | 840 and with weight-3/2 forms (Shimura lifts) where class numbers do appear.

title: minz(p) is always a multiple of p (p ≤ 2·10⁵)
connection: For every prime p ≤ 2·10⁵ the least possible largest denominator minz(p) ≡ 0 (mod p) (OEIS-style constant-zero transform).
why: If provable it pins the optimal solution's structure: the largest denominator always carries p; could give an extremal-solution parametrisation and a minimal-height bound.
first_step: Try to prove: in any solution of 4/p with largest denominator z, if p ∤ z then z ≥ … > some solution with p | z; else find a counterexample for composite-free p beyond 2·10⁵.

title: minz(p)/p sequence: 1,1,2,2,3,4,6,3,6,8,8,10,… (not in OEIS)
connection: floor(minz(p)/p) at primes; at p≡1(4): 2,4,6,8,10,4,14,9,10,8,28,7,…; minz(p)/p correlates −0.42 with τ(4p+1) and −0.31 with R(p).
why: The cofactor of p in the optimal denominator is a 'height' of the cheapest certificate; small values relate to (★) with small C (divisors of 4Cp+1).
first_step: Identify minz(p)/p with the least C such that 4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4C) or similar; test equality over our range.

title: Height growth: max_{p≤X} minz(p)/p
connection: Record values of minz(p) occur at 2,3,5,7,11,13,17,23,29,31,37,53,… (nearly every prime early on); record minz(p)/p would measure the worst certificate height.
why: An upper bound minz(p) ≤ p^{1+θ} for all p is equivalent to ES with a height bound; empirical θ guides which 'bounded C' statement to aim for.
first_step: Compute max_{p ≤ X} log(minz(p)/p)/log p for X up to 10⁷ and fit.

title: U(p) vs smoothness of p−1: ρ(P⁺(p−1) exponent) = +0.40
connection: log P⁺(p−1)/log p correlates +0.40 with U(p) residual: smooth p−1 ⇒ hard.
why: Smooth shifted primes have positive density for P⁺(p−1) ≤ p^{0.2961} (Baker–Harman, cited in FORCED_WINDOW.md); ES-hard primes may be concentrated there, which is a thin set amenable to separate treatment.
first_step: Estimate density of 'ES-hard' (ratio below 0.3) among primes with P⁺(p−1) ≤ p^{1/3} vs others.

title: U₁₂(p)/U₄(p): the 3-divisible fraction of ES solutions
connection: U₁₂(p) counts solutions of 4/p with 3 | x,y,z; its ratio to U₄(p) is a 3-adic local statistic; failures at 193, 577, 2521 mean this fraction hits 0 at hard primes.
why: Factorisation of the count into local factors (Euler product over divisibility conditions) would be a strong structural fingerprint (Manin-type).
first_step: Compute E[U_{4k}(p)/U₄(p)] for k=2,3,5 and compare with 1/k³-type local densities on the ES surface.

title: Neumann–Setzer primes p = u² + 64 among hard primes?
connection: For prime conductor p ≠ 17, elliptic curves with a rational 2-torsion point exist iff p = u² + 64 (Neumann–Setzer; conductor 17 is the exception, LMFDB 17.a); check whether ES-hard primes or R-zeros are of this form (e.g. 409 − 64 = 345 is not a square; 577 − 64 = 513 not).
why: LMFDB fingerprint: an ES ↔ elliptic-curve-of-conductor-p link would show up as over-representation of p = u²+64 among hard primes.
first_step: Test all 14 R-zeros, 3 Type-A failures and the 40 hardest primes for p = u²+64; and correlate U(p) with #isogeny classes of conductor p in LMFDB.

title: Number of elliptic curves of conductor p (or 4p, 8p, 16p) vs U(p)
connection: LMFDB lists curves by conductor; their number at N = p, 2p, 4p, 8p, 16p could correlate with ES counts if ES surfaces fibre into genus-1 curves (cf. GEOMETRY_ES.md) of these conductors.
why: Fibrations of the ES cubic surface by conics/genus-1 curves have discriminants involving p; the Mordell–Weil ranks of such fibres might govern solution counts.
first_step: Download LMFDB conductor counts for N ≤ 500 000 (Cremona tables) and correlate with U(p) residual at p ≤ 30 000 (N=16p).

title: minz(p)/p anticorrelates with h(−4p)/√p (−0.19)
connection: The cheapest certificate is lower (smaller height) when L(1,χ_{−4p}) is large.
why: Height of the optimal solution relates to the (★)/Type II side (χ_{−4p}); a height bound and an L-value bound may be linked.
first_step: Regress log(minz(p)/p) on log L(1,χ_{−4p}) and log L(1,χ_p).

title: Height: every prime ≤ 10⁵ has a solution with z ≤ p², but 50 primes need z > p^{1.75}
connection: z ≤ p² never fails; z ≤ p^{1.75} fails at 50 primes (241, 269, 367, 449, 577, 601, …, last 95327); z ≤ p^{1.5} fails at 7 109 primes.
why: A height-bounded ES ('z ≤ p²') is a finite search per prime with a clean conjectural exponent between 1.75 and 2 — the right scale for effective/lattice approaches (LATTICE_MEETING.md).
first_step: Compute max_{p≤X} log(minz(p))/log p up to 10⁷ and check whether it tends to 2 from below.

title: Primitive solutions (gcd(x,y,z) = 1) fail at 110 primes ≤ 10⁵, all ≡ 1 (mod 12)
connection: No primitive ES solution at 13, 37, 97, 181, 193, 277, 373, 541, 673, 757, 853, 1033, 1093, 1297, 1621, … (last ≤ 10⁵: 98713); share of primitive solutions 7.9%.
why: Primitive points on the ES cubic surface are the integral-point problem proper; failures concentrated on p ≡ 1 (12) show the 3-adic and 4-adic local structure of primitivity.
first_step: Check that all 110 are ≡ 1 (mod 12) and compute failure density in that class (≈ 110/1200?); likely infinite — record as 'primitive ES fails infinitely often?' question.

title: Shares of solution shapes at primes ≈ constants: x | z 0.377, none-div-by-3 0.346, none-div-by-4 0.301, none-div-by-8 0.59, none-div-by-9 0.70
connection: Mean share (over p ≡ 1 (4) > 1000) of each restricted shape among all solutions; these are local-density-like constants of the ES solution set.
why: Stable shares across p would mean the solution set equidistributes in these local conditions (Manin-type equidistribution on the surface) — compare with local densities computed mod 3, 4, 8, 9.
first_step: Compute shares per dyadic range to see whether they converge; compute the local densities predicted by counting solutions mod q.

title: k-term sibling: 4/p as a sum of 3 unit fractions with all denominators ≤ C·p (bounded height)
connection: The smallest C such that every prime ≤ X has a solution with z ≤ C·p^{a} — with a = 2 every prime ≤ 10⁵ works; find the minimal constant for a = 2 (C = max minz(p)/p²).
why: Effective ES with explicit height is what lattice/geometry-of-numbers approaches would produce; the empirical C is the target.
first_step: Done: max minz(p)/p² = 0.5026 at p = 577 (see the effective-height item); extend to windows at 10⁶, 10⁷.

title: Effective height: minz(p) ≤ 0.503·p² for every prime 100 < p ≤ 2·10⁵, extremal at the R-zero 577
connection: max minz(p)/p² = 0.5026 at p = 577 (an R-zero); for p > 1000 the largest log minz/log p is 1.84 (at 6271).
why: An explicit effective-height ES (z ≤ 0.503 p²; minz(577) = 167 330 = 0.50260·577²) holds in range; the extremal prime is again a campaign hard prime, so the height of the cheapest certificate is a hardness detector.
first_step: Track max minz(p)/p² in windows at 10⁶, 10⁷ (count program already outputs minz).

title: Birational chart comparison
connection: Cover the ES surface by different rational charts and compare where integer points have manageable denominators.
why: One chart can hide integrality that another makes explicit.
first_step: Write charts obtained by solving for x, y, and a denominator ratio; compare their divisibility conditions.

title: Height functions on certificates
connection: Compare max(x,y,z), xyz, and auxiliary-parameter height as costs on the same certificate space.
why: A proof-producing descent may work for a height unrelated to the smallest denominator.
first_step: For bounded triples, build move graphs and test which heights decrease along known identity transformations.

title: Logarithmic denominator coordinates
connection: Map triples to log(x),log(y),log(z), comparing thin certificate families with the curved positive ES surface.
why: Multiplicative scales become additive and can expose regions systematically missed by bounded boxes.
first_step: Plot normalized log-denominator triples for primes below 1000 using several search cutoffs.

title: Conic bundles
connection: Choose auxiliary coordinates that leave a conic equation over one parameter and study its local solvability and integral points.
why: Conics admit explicit parametrizations once a rational point is supplied.
first_step: Search linear substitutions that make one residual equation quadratic in two remaining variables.

title: Rational reconstruction
connection: Use modular solutions plus height bounds to reconstruct candidate rational parametrizations of ES certificates.
why: Rational reconstruction is an exact computational tool when the bounds are justified.
first_step: For a fixed prime, reconstruct small ratios y/z from modular solutions at successively larger moduli.

title: Multivariate certificate generating functions
connection: Weight certificates by denominator height, gcd type, and parameter size in a formal generating series.
why: Different projections of one series can compare search costs and arithmetic strata.
first_step: Compute a truncated series for p=13 and inspect which coefficients are invariant under denominator permutation.

title: Toric ideals of monomial substitutions
connection: Encode multiplicative relations among denominator components as binomial equations and study their toric moves.
why: Toric structure may organize equivalent factorizations without confusing them with the additive ES condition.
first_step: For one gcd parametrization, list its monomial map and derive elementary binomial relations.

title: Termination orders for identity search
connection: Seek a well-founded monomial or lexicographic order that decreases under selected ES transformations.
why: A genuine termination argument could turn heuristic rewriting into a reliable normalization procedure.
first_step: Try lexicographic orders on denominator height and gcd data for three verified rewrite rules.

title: Search-budget phase diagrams
connection: Plot witness existence and multiplicity against two independent cutoffs, such as C and allowed denominator height.
why: A two-dimensional diagram may distinguish families that look identical under a single budget.
first_step: For a fixed prime sample, compute coarse grids of success rates over both cutoffs.

title: Adelic height bookkeeping
connection: Combine real denominator size with p-adic valuation penalties in a single explicitly defined height.
why: A balanced height might reveal a descent invisible to the archimedean maximum alone.
first_step: Define a height on one rational parametrization and calculate its change under two exact transformations.

title: Elliptic-curve factorization as a probe
connection: Use small factoring budgets to sample auxiliary factors and ask whether easily found factors already yield many certificates.
why: This measures whether complete factorization is unnecessary for exploratory coverage.
first_step: Apply equal small ECM budgets to a bounded list of auxiliary values and verify all certificates obtained from partial factorizations.

title: Symbolic regression of witness costs
connection: Fit simple formulas for least auxiliary size using arithmetic features rather than raw prime magnitude alone.
why: The goal is a testable growth conjecture or selector, not numerical evidence of universal existence.
first_step: Restrict symbolic regression to a small grammar and validate predictions on a disjoint prime range.

title: Degree profiles versus denominator heights
connection: Classify polynomial certificates by the three denominator degrees and compare them with logarithmic integer heights.
why: Degree balance can expose cancellation regimes that are difficult to see in numerical size data.
first_step: Enumerate degree profiles in a small odd-characteristic model and derive the leading-coefficient cancellation conditions.

title: Boundary divisors and integral points
connection: Compactify a rational parametrization and identify which boundary components correspond to zero, infinite, or nonintegral denominators.
why: The boundary may explain why rational abundance does not directly imply useful integer points.
first_step: For one explicit chart, homogenize its equation and label every boundary component by its arithmetic meaning.

title: Torsor coordinates for gcd removal
connection: Introduce auxiliary variables to encode pairwise coprimality and factor allocation, seeking a torsor-like parametrization.
why: Such coordinates may separate multiplicative structure from the main additive equation.
first_step: Starting from a gcd-stratified triple, write all auxiliary factors and prove the reconstruction map is exact on one stratum.

title: Real components and positivity chambers
connection: Partition the real auxiliary variety by signs of all denominator factors and analyze each chamber separately.
why: Only certain chambers yield positive unit fractions; chamber transitions may suggest controlled transformations.
first_step: For a two-parameter rational family, draw the zero sets of denominator factors and label every positive chamber.

title: Determinant-method maps of certificate concentration
connection: Use low-degree polynomial relations to describe where bounded certificates cluster on the surface.
why: A concentration theorem or experiment could suggest missing parametrizations rather than serve as a reason to discard a route.
first_step: Fit low-degree curves to a bounded set of exact points and check containment symbolically before consulting determinant-method estimates.

title: Lyapunov-function approach: a potential Φ(x,y,z;n) that strictly decreases under an explicit integer move until a solution is reached
connection: Many existence proofs (e.g. Fermat descent, Vieta jumping, Zagier's one-sentence proof structure) are 'potential + move'. Design a potential on near-solutions of 4/n and a move that decreases it.
why: If a move with a monotone potential exists on a finite set, termination = existence. The known failure at squares must show up as the move being undefined there.
first_step: Take near-solutions (x,y,z) with |4/n − Σ 1/x_i| minimal and try candidate moves (replace z by the nearest integer making the sum exact, then rebalance); check empirically whether any simple rule reaches a solution for all p ≤ 10⁴.

title: Union-find / disjoint-set structure of 'solution sharing' between different primes
connection: Two primes share a template if the same (c,d) with the forced f gives solutions for both. Build the graph on primes ≤ X with edges = shared template; connected components and their growth describe how 'global' the solution structure is.
why: Giant-component formation would indicate a Markoff-like 'strong approximation' phenomenon; many tiny components would indicate per-prime independence.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵, list templates (c,d) of all solutions, build the bipartite prime–template graph, compute component structure.

title: Fermat's descent / Vieta jumping on U_n via the 'swap two coordinates' and 'reflect in the third' involutions
connection: U_n: 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx). Solving for z: z = nxy/(4xy − n(x+y)); not a quadratic in z, so no Vieta involution in z directly. But in the homogenised cubic surface there may be involutions via lines on the surface (a cubic surface has 27 lines; the lines through a rational point give conic-bundle involutions).
why: Conic-bundle structure on the cubic surface U_n gives a fibration whose fibres are conics; integral points on conics over ℤ are classical (Legendre); a 'descent along conic fibres' is an ES-specific tool not yet tried? (git grep conic).
first_step: Find the 27 lines of the projective closure of U_n (it's singular, so fewer); pick a conic bundle; write the conic over ℚ(t) and the integrality condition; test for p = 1009 whether integer points lie on few conic fibres.

title: Geometry: integral points on the surface 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) as n varies — the threefold X: 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) in (x,y,z,n) and its fibration over n; is X rational? unirational? what are its integral points' densities?
connection: The total space X ⊂ A⁴ is a cubic threefold (linear in n!): n = 4xyz/(xy+yz+zx) — so X ≅ the graph of a rational function on A³: X is rational, integral points = (x,y,z) with (xy+yz+zx) | 4xyz. ES = surjectivity of n: ℤ³_{>0} ∩ X → ℤ_{≥2}. The question 'which integers are values of 4xyz/(xy+yz+zx)' is a 'value set of a rational function at integer points' problem.
why: Reframes ES as the image of an explicit rational map on integer points — related to the theory of 'representation by rational functions' and to Heath-Brown-style counts of integer points on cubic hypersurfaces where the count of points with a given value of n is f(n). The threefold's geometry (it's rational, the fibres are the U_n) gives a 'total count' Σ_{n ≤ N} f(n) via lattice points on X, which is the Elsholtz–Tao estimate; nothing new, but the 'value set of a rational function' literature (e.g. values of x/y + y/z + z/x) might have transferable ideas.
first_step: Search 'integers of the form 4xyz/(xy+yz+zx)' and the similar classical 'x/y + y/z + z/x = n' problem (Bremner–Guy; elliptic curves!): the latter is an elliptic surface where integer values are determined by rank — a structurally different (and solvable) situation. Compare: why does xy+yz+zx | 4xyz NOT reduce to elliptic curves?

title: Saturation number of Cayley's cubic (arXiv:1406.6963) as an almost-prime ES variant
connection: Saturation results show points on Cayley's cubic with coordinates having few prime factors ↔ ES coordinates have p-adic constraints.
why: If one can force coordinates with bounded Ω on Cayley's cubic, the ES fibre version with one coordinate p·t might be a sieve-reachable relaxation.
first_step: Read 1406.6963 abstract; ask whether its method yields points with a coordinate in a prescribed class mod p.

title: Cox ring of the minimal resolution of the Cayley cubic, fibred over n
connection: The Cayley cubic's Cox ring is known explicitly (Derenthal et al. list Cox rings of singular del Pezzo surfaces) ↔ ES fibre is a hyperplane section x3 = const·n.
why: Explicit Cox ring coordinates for this family would give the 'right' variables in which ES might become a norm or divisor problem with new symmetry.
first_step: Look up Derenthal 'Singular del Pezzo surfaces whose universal torsors are hypersurfaces' and identify Cayley's cubic (4A1) entry.

title: Arakelov / heights: ES certificate size as a height and slopes of an arithmetic bundle
connection: Minimal certificate size vs p ↔ successive minima of an Arakelov vector bundle attached to p (Bost's slopes).
why: Slope inequalities give existence of small sections pointwise (Siegel lemma); ES needs a 'section' landing in an integrality cone.
first_step: Model the (u,C) search space as a hermitian ℤ-module and compute slopes for p ≤ 10⁴; compare with minimal certificate heights.

title: Induction on p via 'certificate inheritance' along chains p → (p+1)/2 or similar
connection: Look for maps φ on primes with φ(p) < p such that ES(φ(p)) plus local data ⟹ ES(p) ↔ a descent/induction proof.
why: Most such maps fail (ES isn't hereditary) but checking simple candidate maps on data is cheap; a map that works empirically to 10⁸ would be surprising and informative.
first_step: Test candidate maps φ(p) ∈ {(p+3)/4, (p−1)/4 odd part, largest prime factor of p+3} for 'certificate transfer' rules on primes ≤ 10⁶.

title: Hereditary closure: ES(n) ⟹ ES(kn), so only primes matter — dualise: does ES(p) follow from ES of all p·q for many q?
connection: Reverse direction: solutions for pq (q varying prime) that are 'Type I in p' might descend ↔ thick family {pq : q prime} at fixed p.
why: This gives a thick object (all primes q) at fixed p; descent condition must be checked. A 'p-primitive' solution for pq with denominators all divisible by q descends.
first_step: For hard p, compute for q ≤ 1000 solutions of 4/(pq) where q divides all denominators (=> descends) vs other; check whether descending solutions exist exactly when ES(p) has certain types.

title: Wilsch: integral points of bounded height on a log Fano threefold — check if the ES threefold is of that type
connection: Wilsch counted integral points on a specific log Fano threefold with torus-like structure. ES's threefold is a cubic with an (S₃ × scaling) symmetry.
why: A matching asymptotic with explicit leading constant would be a cross-check on ET's log³ constant and on the BM-corrected local densities.
first_step: Check the definition of Wilsch's threefold and whether 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is birational to it or to a toric variety.
refs: unverified: Wilsch, Integral points of bounded height on a log Fano threefold (IMRN 2023?)

title: Hilbert property for integral points (Corvaja–Zannier) applied to the fibration n: X → A¹
connection: ES says the image of X(ℤ)_{>0} under n covers ℤ_{≥2}. Corvaja–Zannier relate the Hilbert property/thin images to fundamental groups. Polynomial-identity families have thin images missing squares (F09).
why: A thin-set theorem explaining why parametrised families must miss square classes would turn F09 into a geometric statement and show what a non-thin covering family must look like.
first_step: Check whether Mordell–Schinzel's impossibility is a special case of a Corvaja–Zannier-type 'images of integral points are thin' statement.
refs: unverified: Corvaja, Zannier 2017, On the Hilbert property and the fundamental group of algebraic varieties (Math. Z.)

title: Scholz–Brauer addition chains: ∀n statement proved on infinite thin families, open in general
connection: l(2^n − 1) ≤ n − 1 + l(n) is proved for many infinite families and verified computationally, open in general — the same 'thin families proved, no density rung' profile as ES (F30, F23).
why: Compare the family-proof techniques (Brauer chains, Hansen chains) with ES's 3·2^s + 1 family proofs; both rely on algebraic structure of 2^s.
first_step: Read Clift's computational verification and check whether the proved families cover a positive density of n.

title: Tian's rank results for congruent-number curves
connection: A family-wide rank argument yields pointwise conclusions for primes in selected classes (F01p,F29,F31), through Selmer and analytic rank structures rather than direct counting.
why: It is a relevant precedent for exploiting prime congruence classes and 2-descent to obtain a universal witness on a thin arithmetic family.
first_step: Verify Tian's exact residue-class rank theorem and identify the Selmer parity input; test for an analogous parity constraint on ES certificate counts.
refs: Y. Tian, Congruent numbers and Heegner points, Camb. J. Math. 2 (2014) 117–161 (arXiv:1210.8231)

title: Smith's positive proportion of congruent numbers via Selmer groups
connection: A positive-proportion theorem for a thin arithmetic property shares ES's local solubility and global integral-witness divide (F06,F07,F31), but is density-level rather than pointwise (F05w).
why: The Selmer-group distribution method could provide a new way to quantify how often arithmetic obstructions vanish in a family of surfaces.
first_step: Check Smith's Selmer distribution theorem hypotheses and ask whether a 2-Selmer-like object exists for the ES cubic surface family.
refs: https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.08479 (A. Smith, The congruent numbers have positive natural density)

title: Markoff-type K3 integral Hasse counterexamples
connection: arXiv:2504.10992 constructs Markoff-type K3 surfaces with Zariski-dense rational points that fail the integral Hasse principle; this matches ES F07/F13/F27 and flips F06-style local solubility into failure of integral points.
why: It is a verified explicit warning that rational density and local solubility do not settle an integral-point problem on a surface. The obstruction there is Brauer–Manin, which Bright–Loughran (arXiv:1908.02526) show is absent for ES, so look for non-BM ingredients.
first_step: Read the counterexample construction and isolate the integral obstruction; test whether its mechanism has an analogue on an ES fixed-n fibre.

title: Integral Hasse failure despite dense rational points
connection: The Markoff-type K3 examples of arXiv:2504.10992 share ES F13/F07 and F21: global integral existence can fail despite abundance at the rational level, unlike the pointwise positive-integer target.
why: This establishes a close negative control for proposed ES arguments that pass from rational parametrization to integral solutions.
first_step: Compare the authors' obstruction with the denominators in a rational parametrization of the ES cubic; determine where integrality is lost.

title: Use Markoff K3 obstructions to audit local tests
connection: The Hasse-failing Markoff-type K3 family in arXiv:2504.10992 shares ES F06/F07/F13 and demonstrates why checking all local conditions need not supply a global integral point.
why: It is a concrete test case against overinterpreting ES's known local solubility.
first_step: Read the local-solubility verification in the paper and list which parts depend on the Markoff form, then test their analogues on ES modulo small prime powers.

title: Markoff-type equations and logarithmic solution growth
connection: The generalized Markov–Hurwitz equations studied in arXiv:2605.05075 share ES F01/F13/F38 and F04w: positive integral surface solutions are organized by nonlinear equation structure and have a reported logarithmic asymptotic phenomenon.
why: The specific asymptotic theorem may inform how orbit size and witness counts behave in a Diophantine surface family.
first_step: Check the theorem's exact solution-counting variable and determine whether any ES parametrized subfamily has comparable tree growth.

title: Problem 300: Croot construction as a thin-set stress test
connection: Problem 300 ↔ ES F04, F05, F12, F24: sparse representation counts, density bounds and heuristic abundance.
why: A theorem disproving the expected scale for reciprocal subset representations is a reminder to test ES heuristics against deliberately sparse constructions.
first_step: Use the construction cited on the page to build a restricted denominator set and calculate whether its induced ES candidate count is atypically small.

title: Scholz–Brauer: inductive addition-chain constructions
connection: The Scholz conjecture shares F01,F16w,F23,F30: a universal bound is sought, short arithmetic words are certificates, and constructive families establish infinite subcases. ES also has short polynomial certificates and thin proven families.
why: Inductive constructions that append a small chain segment may translate to recursive ES certificate transformations across related n.
first_step: Read the construction for the proved infinite family in the 2023 paper and search for ES maps n↦an+b preserving a unit-fraction certificate.

title: Integral points and effective height bounds
connection: Effective integral-point problems share F13, F32 and the tension between small certificates and uniform existence.
why: A bound on minimal witness height polynomial in p could permit a structured search or finite reduction.
first_step: Check known effective bounds for integral points on the ES surface and identify whether they are uniform in the parameter p.

title: Adelic methods for integral points in families
connection: Arithmetic families share F06, F07, F13, F20; local densities may vary with the parameter and influence global integral points.
why: Uniform adelic analysis could identify parameter classes with systematically stronger integral-point counts.
first_step: Compute local densities of ES surface points at primes dividing 2p and compare with the global expected count across p residue classes.

title: Maynard primes with restricted digits → thin sets with Fourier control
connection: Maynard (Invent. 2019) counts primes with a missing decimal digit by strong Fourier bounds on the thin digit set; the set of ES-hard residue patterns (Mordell classes mod 840 and deeper digit-like conditions mod 4C) is a digit-like thin set.
why: Template for proving that a thin, Fourier-structured set of p's must intersect the ES-good set.
first_step: Compute the Fourier transform (mod M = 840·k) of the indicator of 'not covered by identities of modulus ≤ M' and compare its L1 norm with Maynard's digit-set bounds.
refs: Maynard, Primes with restricted digits, Invent. Math. 217 (2019), arXiv:1604.01041

title: U_n's closure is the Cayley 4-nodal cubic σ₃(x,y,z,w)=0 — log CY pair with a triangle through 3 nodes
connection: Substituting w = −4w′/n turns 4xyz = nw(xy+yz+zx) into σ₃(x,y,z,w′) = xyz+w′(xy+yz+zx) = 0, the Cayley cubic (checked: singular exactly at the 4 coordinate points). U_n = Cayley cubic minus the triangle w=0 through three nodes; the Markoff k=4 surface is the same cubic minus a triangle avoiding the nodes.
why: Places ES next to Markoff in the classification of log Calabi–Yau cubic pairs and pins down the one geometric difference (boundary through vs. away from nodes) — any Markoff-type tool must explain what it does at the nodes.
first_step: Write the explicit projective equivalence to x²+y²+z²−xyz = 4 closure and map the U_n boundary triangle and the integral structure (w′ = −n/4) across; record which Markoff automorphisms preserve the ES boundary.
refs: Bright–Loughran, Brauer–Manin obstruction for Erdős–Straus surfaces, Bull. LMS 52 (2020)

title: Reciprocal plane / Orlik–Terao algebra viewpoint
connection: In inverted coordinates (u,v,w) = (1/x,1/y,1/z), U_n is the plane u+v+w = 4/n; its closure in the x-coordinates is the reciprocal plane of an affine hyperplane (Proudfoot–Speyer), whose coordinate ring is an Orlik–Terao algebra.
why: Reciprocal linear spaces have explicit Gröbner bases, Hilbert series and degenerations (broken circuits); a combinatorial degeneration could organise integral points.
first_step: Compute the Orlik–Terao / Proudfoot–Speyer presentation for the arrangement {u,v,w,u+v+w−4/n} and see whether integral points correspond to lattice points in a broken-circuit fan.
refs: Proudfoot–Speyer, A broken circuit ring, Beiträge Algebra Geom. 47 (2006)
Kummer–Vinzant, The Chow form of a reciprocal linear space, Michigan Math. J. 68 (2019)

title: Harpaz–Wittenberg fibration method along the x-fibration of U_n
connection: HW prove that the Brauer–Manin obstruction is the only one for fibrations over P¹ whose fibres satisfy it, under a fibration hypothesis (proved in many cases); fixing x gives a fibre ((4x−n)y − nx)((4x−n)z − nx) = (nx)², a split torus-like curve whose integral points are divisors of (nx)².
why: Makes precise the sense in which ES is 'a fibration whose fibres are divisor problems' and which hypothesis (Schinzel/HL-type) would be needed.
first_step: State the HW-type conjecture for integral points of this fibration and identify the exact divisor-problem hypothesis it needs at n = p.
refs: Harpaz–Wittenberg, On the fibration method for zero-cycles and rational points, Ann. Math. 183 (2016), arXiv:1409.0993

title: Harpaz–Skorobogatov–Wittenberg: Hardy–Littlewood (finite complexity) ⇒ rational points on fibrations
connection: HSW use Green–Tao–Ziegler to prove HP for fibrations with split degenerate fibres over linear polynomials; ES fibrations have degenerate fibres over linear forms in x.
why: Unconditional finite-complexity linear prime patterns are available — the cheapest unconditional input to fibration methods.
first_step: Identify the degenerate fibres of U_n → A¹_x and test whether they are 'split over linear polynomials' in HSW's sense.
refs: Harpaz–Skorobogatov–Wittenberg, The Hardy–Littlewood conjecture and rational points, Compositio 150 (2014), arXiv:1304.3333

title: Whang: nonlinear descent on moduli of local systems → is U_n a relative character variety?
connection: Whang proves structure theorems for integral points on moduli of SL₂ local systems on surfaces (Markoff-type) via mapping class group descent; the Cayley cubic is the SL₂ character variety of the four-holed sphere at special boundary traces.
why: If U_n is (an integral model of) a relative character variety, mapping-class-group descent gives finiteness of orbits of integral points.
first_step: Match U_n to the Fricke cubic of the four-holed sphere: find boundary traces (a,b,c,d) making the Fricke cubic projectively equal to 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) with the ES boundary.
refs: Whang, Nonlinear descent on moduli of local systems, arXiv:1710.01848
Whang, Arithmetic of curves on moduli of local systems, arXiv:1803.04583

title: OAI 027 potential integral density on curve character varieties (claimed)
connection: OAI 027 claims integral points become Zariski dense (after finite extension) on SL_n character varieties of curves; if U_n is a character-variety component, potential density of integral points is known type.
why: Potential density is weaker than ES, but structural info about how integral points arise could be imported.
first_step: After the previous item's identification, read OAI 027's mechanism for producing integral points.

title: Uniform dimension growth (Castryck–Cluckers–Dittmann–Nguyen) for upper bounds on f(n)
connection: CCDN prove uniform polynomial-in-degree bounds for rational points of bounded height on projective varieties (determinant method); f(n) is a count of integral points of bounded height on U_n.
why: Uniform upper bounds f(n) ≪ n^ε are inputs for second-moment/variance arguments.
first_step: Compare the CCDN bound applied to U_n with the trivial divisor bound f(n) ≪ n^{ε}; see whether it gives anything uniform in a range of heights.
refs: Castryck–Cluckers–Dittmann–Nguyen, The dimension growth conjecture, polynomial in the degree and without logarithmic factors, arXiv:1904.13109

title: Corvaja–Zannier degeneracy of integral points via the subspace theorem
connection: CZ (Annals 2004) prove non-density of integral points on affine surfaces whose boundary has many components; U_n's boundary has 3 lines (log CY), the borderline case where integral points may be dense.
why: Adding extra boundary (e.g. requiring x,y,z to avoid primes in a set S, i.e. S-integral constraints) pushes into the CZ degenerate regime — giving finiteness of 'too-structured' solution families.
first_step: Determine the number of boundary components needed for CZ when imposing 'xyz is S-smooth' and deduce a finiteness lemma for S-smooth ES solutions across n.
refs: Corvaja–Zannier, On integral points on surfaces, Ann. Math. 160 (2004)

title: Universal torsors of the Cayley cubic for parametrising ES solutions
connection: Integral points on singular del Pezzo surfaces are parametrised via universal torsors (Derenthal, Colliot-Thélène–Sansuc); the Type I/II divisor forms are presumably the torsor equations of U_n.
why: A torsor parametrisation makes integral points into lattice points with coprimality — the setting for geometry-of-numbers and circle-method counts.
first_step: Compute the Cox ring of the minimal resolution of the Cayley cubic (blow-up of P² in 6 points of a complete quadrilateral) and write the torsor equation with the ES boundary.
refs: Derenthal, Singular del Pezzo surfaces whose universal torsors are hypersurfaces, Proc. LMS 108 (2014)

title: Santens / Wilsch integral Manin conjecture applied to U_n
connection: Santens proves Manin's conjecture for integral points on toric varieties; Wilsch counts integral points on log Fano threefolds; Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel give the predicted shape. f(n) is a count of integral points on the log CY U_n (not log Fano) with growing n.
why: The log CY case predicts polylog growth — matching M_BM ≍ log²; an integral-Manin framework could give a conceptual main term.
first_step: Compute Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel's predicted exponent of log B for integral points on the Cayley cubic minus triangle and compare with log² p.
refs: Santens, Manin's conjecture for integral points on toric varieties, arXiv:2312.13914
Wilsch, Integral points of bounded height on a log Fano threefold, arXiv:1901.08503

title: Browning–Le Boudec–Sawin: Hasse principle for random Fano hypersurfaces
connection: BLS prove HP for 100% of Fano hypersurfaces of fixed degree and dimension ordered by height; ES gives a one-parameter family (in n), not a random family.
why: Calibrates: one-parameter families are exactly where 'random family' methods do not apply.
first_step: Record the family dimension needed in BLS's argument and compare with the ES family {U_n} (dimension 1).
refs: Browning–Le Boudec–Sawin, The Hasse principle for random Fano hypersurfaces, Ann. Math. 197 (2023), arXiv:2006.02356

title: Mordell–Weil / elliptic fibrations on the Cayley cubic resolution
connection: The minimal resolution of the Cayley cubic is a weak del Pezzo of degree 3; pencils of anticanonical sections give elliptic fibrations whose fibres carry group laws.
why: Group laws on fibres could produce new ES solutions from old (chord–tangent) with integrality tracked — a source of solution-generating operations.
first_step: Pick a pencil of plane sections through a node, compute the elliptic fibration, and test whether adding a torsion section maps integral ES points to integral ES points.

title: Cremona symmetries of the Cayley cubic and ES solution moves
connection: The Cayley cubic's automorphism/birational symmetry group includes S₄ on the nodes and quadratic Cremona maps (inversion x ↦ 1/x relates to the reciprocal plane); ES only uses S₃ permutations.
why: Any extra symmetry preserving the integral structure would give the missing ES 'group action' (cf. Chen/Markoff).
first_step: List the birational automorphisms of σ₃ = 0 commuting with w′ = const and test their action on ES solutions for small n.

title: Motivic / Grothendieck-ring class of U_n and its point counts
connection: The class [U_n] in K₀(Var) and its point counts #U_n(𝔽_ℓ) are computable (Cayley cubic minus triangle); integral-point main terms are built from such local counts.
why: Exact point counts mod ℓ give exact local densities and identify any 'local sterility' structure for free.
first_step: Compute #U_n(𝔽_ℓ) symbolically as a function of n mod ℓ and verify it's ℓ² − 3ℓ + c(n,ℓ) style.

title: Integral points on hyperplane-arrangement complements (very affine varieties) via tropical compactification
connection: The torus part of U_n (all coordinates nonzero) is P² minus 4 lines in reciprocal coordinates — a very affine variety; tropical compactifications (Tevelev) and Huh's likelihood geometry study such varieties.
why: Tropicalisation shows which valuation patterns (sizes of x,y,z relative to n) integral points can have — a size-pattern classification of ES solutions.
first_step: Compute the tropical variety of the reciprocal plane and compare its cones with the observed (log x, log y, log z)/log n patterns of ES solutions at p ≤ 10^6.
refs: Tevelev, Compactifications of subvarieties of tori, Amer. J. Math. 129 (2007)
Huh, The maximum likelihood degree of a very affine variety, Compositio 149 (2013)

title: Pila–Shankar–Tsimerman André–Oort heights for the CM tetrahedron of the Cayley cubic
connection: PST proved André–Oort via canonical height bounds; the Cayley cubic/Markoff CM dictionary in the repo (cayley_markoff_cm) relates special points to CM data.
why: Height bounds for special points might constrain which CM points carry ES solutions (a finiteness/distribution statement).
first_step: Locate the CM-point parametrisation in cayley_markoff_cm.md and check whether ES integral points map to special points of bounded height.
refs: Pila–Shankar–Tsimerman, Canonical heights on Shimura varieties and the André–Oort conjecture, arXiv:2109.08788

title: OAI 002/030 BSD formula & modularity over imaginary quadratic fields (claimed) — ES has no elliptic curve
connection: These claimed results concern elliptic curves; ES's surface is rational (Cayley cubic) with no natural attached elliptic curve except via chosen fibrations.
why: Null result recorded; the only conceivable link is through elliptic fibrations of the Cayley cubic resolution (separate item).
first_step: Close.

title: Markov/Markoff via cluster algebra of the once-punctured torus — ES analogue?
connection: Markoff triples are cluster variables of the once-punctured torus cluster algebra; the Cayley cubic ↔ four-punctured sphere character variety; ES's U_n shares the Cayley cubic.
why: If U_n's integral points are cluster-like for the four-punctured sphere (Fomin–Shapiro–Thurston surface cluster algebras), mutation provides the missing group action.
first_step: Compute the cluster algebra of the four-punctured sphere and its exchange relations; test whether ES solution triples satisfy any mutation relation.
refs: Fomin–Shapiro–Thurston, Cluster algebras and triangulated surfaces I, Acta Math. 201 (2008)

title: Siegel's theorem on integral points of curves for one-parameter ES slices
connection: A curve C ⊂ U_n (e.g. x fixed as polynomial in a parameter) has infinitely many integral points only if genus 0 with ≤ 2 points at infinity; ES certificate curves are genus 0 with specific boundary.
why: Counting points at infinity classifies which 1-parameter certificate families can be infinite — a structural census.
first_step: For each certificate family in the repo, compute genus and number of points at infinity of the associated curve.
refs: Siegel, Über einige Anwendungen diophantischer Approximationen (1929)

title: Brauer–Manin for the pencil S_{n,k} at k = −4 (sibling failures {2,9,21,165,945,1197})
connection: The repo proved a BM obstruction on S_{n,k} for positive squares k; at k = −4 failures exist but no invariant is known; Colliot-Thélène–Xu style integral BM with negative k is untried.
why: Explaining sibling failures by a BM class would refine the zero-law calibration and test whether ES-type failures are always 'lottery'.
first_step: Compute Br S_{n,−4} and evaluate the candidate quaternion classes at the failing n.
refs: Colliot-Thélène–Xu, Brauer–Manin obstruction for integral points of homogeneous spaces and representation by integral quadratic forms, Compositio 145 (2009)

title: Gaussian ES_Q1 count growth log³N vs log²N: Lang–Weil / local densities explanation
connection: z52 found ES_Q1 counts grow like log³N (EVIDENCE) against the board's log²N; integral-Manin-type predictions depend on the rank of the relevant Picard/boundary data over ℚ(i).
why: A geometric explanation (extra boundary component splitting over ℚ(i)) would validate the log-power heuristics used for ES itself.
first_step: Compute the Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel exponent for U_n over ℚ(i) vs ℚ (Galois action on boundary/nodes) and compare with 3 vs 2.
refs: Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel, Igusa integrals and volume asymptotics in analytic and adelic geometry, Confluentes Math. 2 (2010)

title: Quantitative Hilbert irreducibility (Cohen; Castillo–Dietmann) for ES certificate covers
connection: Quantitative HIT bounds the number of specialisations where a Galois group drops; ES certificate covers over the p-line have Galois groups whose specialisations at p determine certificate existence.
why: If the cover's Galois group stays large at all but few p, Chebotarev-type positivity follows for most p — and exceptional p are 'thin sets'.
first_step: Compute the Galois group of a single Type I certificate cover (fixed c,d) over ℚ(p) and its thin-set exceptions.
refs: Castillo–Dietmann, On Hilbert's irreducibility theorem, Acta Arith. 180 (2017)

title: Hacking–Prokhorov degenerations of P² to P(a²,b²,c²) and Markov-type equations for ES
connection: Hacking–Prokhorov: toric degenerations of P² to weighted projective planes with T-singularities are governed by Markov triples a²+b²+c² = 3abc, generated by mutations. ES's Markoff-type surface S_{n,D}: nA²+B²+D = ABC is a twisted analogue.
why: Mutation trees of degenerations give an infinite combinatorial structure over a Markov-type equation, and U_n has no comparable mutation structure (only coordinate permutations), while S_{n,D} has only Vieta-type involutions such as B ↦ AC − B (and A ↦ BC/n − A when n | BC). This is a place to look for a hidden mutation.
first_step: Check whether S_{n,D} solutions arise as weights of Q-Gorenstein degenerations of some del Pezzo (degree depending on n); start from HP's classification table.

title: A¹-curves on U_n and log Gromov–Witten counts vs polynomial ES identities
connection: GHK's theta functions are built from counts of A¹-curves (log GW invariants) meeting the boundary at one point. Integral A¹-curves in U_n are polynomial parametric families of (signed) solutions, the fixed-n analogue of Mordell identities.
why: Mordell–Schinzel says no polynomial families cover square classes. Log GW counts are an enumerative invariant of the same objects, so they might give a geometric reason for which classes are covered.
first_step: Count low-degree A¹-curves on U_n for a few n by direct polynomial search (deg ≤ 3); compare with the GHK broken-line counts.

title: Harpaz's log K3 surfaces: dP5 minus a pentagon and the frieze variety with coefficient N
connection: Harpaz classified log K3 surfaces with trivial geometric Picard group compactifiable to del Pezzos: dP5 with a boundary pentagon of (−1)-curves, which is the A₂ cluster variety. He proved non-Zariski-density of integral points when the Galois action is trivial. The ES₅ frieze (Ptolemy relations with frozen sides (1,1,1,1,N)) is a one-parameter deformation of this variety.
why: It is the closest proved arithmetic theorem about integral points on the exact variety class carrying ES₅ words, and it shows how Brauer–Manin fails to be the only obstruction there.
first_step: Check whether the N-fibre of the pentagon-with-coefficients variety is again dP5 minus a pentagon (a twisted A₂ cluster variety), and read Harpaz §§4–5 for the non-BM obstruction mechanism.
refs: arXiv:1511.01285 (Harpaz, Geometry and arithmetic of certain log K3 surfaces)

title: Integral points on log CY surfaces: counting conjecture of order (log B)^k and the U_n fibre
connection: For log K3/log CY surfaces the expected integral point count up to height B is a power of log B (Harpaz; Wilsch-type works on integral points of bounded height). U_n has finitely many positive points, but its signed integral points can be counted.
why: The ES expected count ≍ log²n matches 'log-power' heuristics for log CY. Translating the n-dependence into height may connect ES's count to a Manin-type conjecture for integral points.
first_step: Count signed integral points on U_n of height ≤ B for fixed n and growing B (numerically); compare with a (log B)^b law and identify b with the boundary's dual-complex dimension.
refs: Wilsch, Integral points of bounded height on a log Fano threefold (check arXiv)

title: Total family U → A¹_n: integral points on a threefold and Manin–Peyre for the total space
connection: The total space 𝒰 = {4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx)} ⊂ A⁴ is a threefold. ES says the projection 𝒰(ℤ_{>0}) → ℤ_{≥2} is surjective. Integral points on the threefold are counted asymptotically (Elsholtz–Tao averages), so surjectivity is a 'fibre-wise' strengthening.
why: This is the standard 'surjectivity of a morphism on integral points' question, related to Serre's thin-set / Hilbert irreducibility for integral points. The fibres here are log CY rather than rational curves.
first_step: Look up results on 'integral points: surjectivity onto the base' (e.g. Corvaja–Zannier thin sets, integral Hilbert irreducibility) to locate the nearest theorem.
refs: Corvaja–Zannier, On the Hilbert property and the fundamental group (check)

title: The pencil S_{n,k}: 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) = k as a K3-type family with a singular fibre at k = 0
connection: Z52 proved a BM obstruction for k = m² (with congruence conditions) that dies at k = 0. In degeneration theory, the k = 0 fibre is the central fibre of a family of affine cubic surfaces. Brauer classes can extend over the family or ramify at k = 0.
why: Specialisation of Brauer classes in families (purity/residue maps) is a native tool. The residue along the exceptional conic was computed; nearby fibres give limiting information.
first_step: Compute Br of the generic fibre of the pencil over Q(k), and the residues at k = 0 and k = ∞; record whether any class survives as an unramified class on the k = 0 fibre's resolution.

title: Integral points via the universal torsor: ES as lattice points satisfying a system of coprime divisibilities
connection: Torsor descent turns 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) into the classical parametrisation x = abd·…, which has the shape of ET's (a,b,c,d) Type I/II data. Torsor coordinates are the standard native coordinates.
why: It explains the ET parametrisations as torsor coordinates, and opens the use of the torsor's own symmetry group, a torus.
first_step: Match ET (2.1)–(2.7) with the Cox ring of the minimal desingularisation of the closure; list any extra torus action not used so far.
refs: Derenthal, Cox rings of singular del Pezzo surfaces (check)

title: Integral Hasse principle for U_n relative to a group action at infinity (ℝ⁺ component)
connection: BL treat the positive real component U_n(ℝ)⁺. Positivity of solutions is an archimedean condition; BM evaluation can see real connected components (as in BL's U_n(ℝ)⁺ version), but not finer positivity structure inside a component. Strong approximation with an archimedean constraint is studied for homogeneous spaces.
why: The repo's T1 is a reciprocity obstruction coupling the archimedean and finite places. The native tool is a 'Brauer–Manin with archimedean condition' (BL's U(ℝ)⁺ version).
first_step: Re-read BL §§5–7 for the exact role of U_n(ℝ)⁺; record which Brauer classes have non-constant evaluation on U_n(ℝ)⁺.

title: Elliptic fibration of the ES cubic by planes x + y + z = s
connection: Intersecting the projective closure with the pencil of planes x + y + z = sw gives plane cubic curves, an elliptic fibration (after base-point blow-ups). ES points are integral points on these elliptic curves with positive coordinates.
why: The elliptic-curve toolbox applies fibrewise: Mordell–Weil ranks, Néron–Tate heights and integral points. Ranks along the family could produce infinitely many signed points.
first_step: Compute the Weierstrass model of the s-fibre for fixed n (sympy), and the Mordell–Weil rank of the generic fibre over Q(s).

title: Conic bundle over the x-line: Châtelet-surface toolbox (descent, Schinzel's hypothesis)
connection: The x-fibration is a conic bundle with split degenerate fibres. Châtelet surfaces and conic bundles have Hasse principle results conditional on Schinzel's hypothesis (Colliot-Thélène–Sansuc–Swinnerton-Dyer) and unconditional ones in some degrees (Browning–Matthiesen–Skorobogatov).
why: It is the canonical way the field produces points fibrewise. Integral and positivity constraints are what is missing, but the fibration method with additive combinatorics (Green–Tao input) is a powerful modern variant.
first_step: Write the x-fibration's degenerate fibres as linear forms in x. Check whether Browning–Matthiesen–Skorobogatov's linear-forms setting applies to integral points with x in a short range.
refs: Browning–Matthiesen–Skorobogatov, Rational points on pencils of conics and quadrics with many degenerate fibres (Ann. Math. 2014)

title: Vojta/abc for integral points on U_n: what does 'log Kodaira dimension 0' predict
connection: Vojta's conjecture predicts degeneracy of integral points only for log general type. U_n is log CY (κ̄ = 0), so integral points may be dense, and no prediction of existence follows.
why: This is a calibration: it explains why no conjectural Diophantine machine gives ES, unlike Markoff (log CY too) where Ghosh–Sarnak found failures.
first_step: Note as calibration. Check whether 'log CY with BM set non-empty but positive points absent' is known to occur infinitely often in a family (Loughran–Mitankin for Markoff).
refs: Loughran–Mitankin, Integral Hasse principle and strong approximation for Markoff surfaces (IMRN 2021; check)

title: Motivic/Igusa zeta function of U_n: local densities and the BM main term
connection: The BM main term is a product of local densities, each the limit of #U_n(ℤ/p^k)/p^{2k}. Igusa's local zeta function encodes these densities as rational functions with poles governed by an embedded resolution.
why: The exact local factors (especially at 2) control the T1/sign phenomena. Igusa poles might give a uniform closed form for the BM constant, which is already exact.
first_step: Compute Igusa zeta of 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) at p = 2 and p | n via the toric resolution; compare with BM_CORRECTED_COUNT local factors.

title: Hasse principle for the 'Type II at fixed level' variety: d | 4Cn+1, d ≡ −1 (mod 4C) as a norm-form/torus variety
connection: At fixed C, a solution is a factorisation 4Cn+1 = d·d′ with d ≡ −1 (mod 4C). This is an integral point on a torus-type variety (norm form for the trivial extension, with level structure). Ray-class-field reciprocity says the class of d is constrained.
why: Torus-variety integral points with level structure are governed by class field theory (ray class groups). ES at fixed C is exactly a ray-class question, B2.
first_step: Record the ray class group mod 4C whose Frobenius class decides it, and the explicit list of p's covered for C ≤ 20 (sanity link to Mordell covering).

title: Markoff-type surface S_{n,D}: Vieta jumping (olympiad technique) as a descent on certificates
connection: S_{n,D}: nA² + B² + D = ABC has the Vieta involution B ↦ AC − B (always integral) and A ↦ BC/n − A (integral only when n | BC). Where the involutions stay integral and positive, Vieta jumping descends solutions towards fundamental ones (IMO 1988 Q6 style); unrestricted integral descent is not automatic here.
why: Vieta jumping is the elementary native tool for Markoff-type equations. It gives finite fundamental sets per (n, D) and transports positivity along orbits.
first_step: For n = p < 500, compute the fundamental (minimal) solutions under Vieta jumping on S_{p,D} and check whether ES certificates (2D | C) appear among fundamental solutions or in their orbits.

title: ES₅ words as integral points of a twisted M₀,₅ (A₂ cluster surface birational to M₀,₅)
connection: The A₂ cluster variety is M₀,₅ (configurations of 5 points on P¹), up to passing to open subsets (the A2 cluster surface is dP5 minus a pentagon of lines, whereas M_{0,5} is dP5 minus all ten boundary lines, so the relationship is birational/open-subset, not equality). Positive integral friezes correspond to special integral points. The coefficient-N pentagon is a twist/deformation. Integral points of M₀,₅ over ℤ[1/S] are governed by S-unit equations.
why: This brings the S-unit equation toolbox (finiteness, effective bounds, counting) and the cross-ratio coordinates of M₀,₅ to ES₅ words.
first_step: Write the five frieze entries as cross-ratios of 5 points on P¹ and identify the N-twist; check whether words correspond to points of M₀,₅ with cross-ratios in a multiplicative set related to N.

title: s-form: ES(p) ⇔ ∃ s ∈ ℕ³ with lcm_i 4s_i/gcd(4s_i, S) = p (value of an arithmetic function)
connection: GEOMETRY_ES: positive points ↔ primitive s with 4s_i | nS, and ES(p) ⟺ ∃ s with m(s) = lcm_i 4s_i/gcd(4s_i,S) = p. ES says the arithmetic function m on primitive triples hits every prime.
why: Surjectivity of an explicit arithmetic function on ℕ³ is the native form for additive/multiplicative combinatorics (value sets of lcm/gcd expressions, like the problem of values of lcm(a,b)/gcd(a,b)-type maps).
first_step: Compute the distribution of m(s) over s ≤ B and the smallest-height s with m(s) = p for p < 10⁶; look at the gcd(4s_i, S) pattern of minimal solutions.

title: Square-tiled surfaces with p squares: cylinder decompositions ↔ words
connection: Origamis (square-tiled surfaces) with p squares have cylinder decompositions with heights, widths and twists satisfying Σ h_i w_i = p. A 3-cylinder decomposition with parameters (t,u,v)-type could encode tuv − u − v = p and the sign as a monodromy-group property.
why: Origami monodromy groups (subgroups of S_p) have classifications. 'Monodromy contains an odd permutation' style conditions are Legendre-type (Zolotarev: (A/p) is the sign of x ↦ Ax on ℤ/p).
first_step: Using Zolotarev's lemma, (A/p) = sign of the permutation x ↦ Ax mod p. Look for an origami with p squares whose horizontal/vertical permutations are x ↦ x+1 and x ↦ Ax, and whose cylinder structure encodes the word.

title: Markov uniqueness at prime powers (Baragar, Button, Schmutz) as a pointwise-at-primes precedent
connection: The Markov uniqueness conjecture is proved when the largest Markov number is a prime power (Baragar; Button; Schmutz), using the factorisation/roots of x² ≡ −1 (mod m) and the arithmetic of 9m² − 4. It is a pointwise statement at primes about a Markoff-type equation, proved via the arithmetic of a p-tied integer.
why: It is a rare (R)-type rigidity result at primes for a Markoff-type surface; ES's S_{n,D} is Markoff-type. Its mechanism (counting square roots of −1 mod p) is cheap and might transfer to counting certificate roots mod p.
first_step: Read Button, 'The uniqueness of the prime Markoff numbers' (J. LMS 1998); identify the step where primality is used and check whether an analogous root count constrains S_{p,D} solutions.
refs: Button, The uniqueness of the prime Markoff numbers (J. LMS 1998)
Aigner, Markov's Theorem and 100 Years of the Uniqueness Conjecture (2013)

title: SL₂-character variety of the punctured torus / pair of pants: S_{n,D} as a relative character variety
connection: Markoff-type cubics x² + y² + z² − xyz = k are relative SL₂-character varieties of the once-punctured torus (k = boundary trace + 2). The mapping class group acts, and that action drives BGS/Chen. S_{n,D} might be a character variety of a different surface or with a twisted boundary condition, or might not be one at all.
why: If S_{n,D} is a (twisted) character variety, a mapping-class-group action exists, which is exactly the missing infinite group action; if not, that is a structural reason for the difference from Markoff.
first_step: Test whether nA² + B² + D − ABC can be transformed (rescaling, sign changes over ℚ(√n)) into a character-variety cubic x² + y² + z² − xyz − k; compute the invariants (discriminant, singular points) to decide.
refs: Goldman, The modular group action on real SL(2)-characters of a one-holed torus (Geom. Topol. 2003)

title: Algebraic geometry of the word surface W: tuv − u − v = p as a cubic surface family over the p-line
connection: W_p : tuv − u − v = p is an affine cubic surface (a log CY of the same 'xyz + linear' type as Markoff-like surfaces). Its integral points are words. Its Brauer group and BM obstruction for integral points with the sign condition give an ES₅-native arithmetic-geometry statement.
why: It gives ES₅ its own arithmetic geometry, distinct from U_n, possibly with a cleaner Brauer group (the sign condition might be a Brauer class evaluation).
first_step: Compute Br(W_p) for the compactification (sympy/Magma); test whether (A/p) = (tu − 1 / p) is the evaluation of a quaternion algebra class (ramified along tu = 1; see the Brauer item) (tu − 1, p) on W_p.

title: Brauer class (tu − 1, p) on the word surface: the ES₅ sign as a Brauer–Manin evaluation
connection: On W_p, the quaternion algebra 𝒜 = (tu − 1, p) defines an Azumaya algebra on the open subset W_p° = {tu ≠ 1}, which contains all positive words; on W_p it is ramified along {tu − 1 = 0} (there u = −p, t = −1/p, and the residue is the non-square class of p), so one must work on W_p° or look for another, unramified class. Its Hilbert symbol at p (local invariant 0 or 1/2) is (tu − 1 / p) = the sign. By the product formula (on W_p°), the sign equals the product of the Hilbert symbols at the other places (2, ∞, q | tu − 1), which is the slot lemma.
why: It would make the slot lemma an instance of Brauer–Manin reciprocity and ES₅ a statement 'some integral point has non-trivial 𝒜-evaluation at p'. This is the integral-points-with-prescribed-Brauer-evaluation problem (studied for Markoff surfaces by Colliot-Thélène–Wei–Xu).
first_step: Confirm the ramification of (tu − 1, p) along tu = 1 and at the boundary of a compactification, and decide whether evaluation on the open set W_p° (a ramified/log Brauer evaluation) is a meaningful obstruction-theoretic statement; compute local evaluation maps at 2 and ∞ and compare with the slot lemma.
refs: Colliot-Thélène–Wei–Xu, Brauer–Manin obstruction for Markoff surfaces (2020; check)

title: g(4)=19 descent: analytic threshold + greedy reduction to the verified range
connection: BDD reduced every n below 10³⁶⁷ to the verified range by subtracting biquadrates. ES has no subtraction structure, but the e-slice form reduces ES(p) to a property of N = (p+e)/4 < p; formalize a 'descent' that moves a hard instance to a smaller one.
why: If certificate existence at p could be read off from data at N ≈ p/4 that is itself verifiable recursively, verification scales.
first_step: Measure: for the hardest primes (DISPROOF_AVENUES list) how many e ≤ 1000 give N = (p+e)/4 with ≥ k divisors; is there always an e with N highly composite?

title: Chord–tangent operations on the ES cubic surface family
connection: Euler's identity is a composition law on norm forms. The ES surface 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is a cubic surface; secant/tangent constructions (Manin) generate rational points from rational points.
why: Rational points are plentiful; the question is whether some composition preserves integrality or near-integrality across fibres n.
first_step: Implement the secant operation on U_n(ℚ) and measure denominators of the third point when the two inputs are integral points of nearby fibres (n, n') with n' | n·k.

title: Power-size main term requirement: lift ES to a variety with power-many points fibred over certificates
connection: Tartakowsky/Kloosterman work because the Eisenstein term ≍ n^{k/2−1} beats cusp-form bounds; ES's main term is log²p. Seek V_p → {ES certificates of p} with fibres of size p^δ (nontrivial geometry), so V_p's point count has a power-size main term that vanishes iff ES(p) fails.
why: Changes the competition 'polylog main term vs. error' into 'power main term vs. error' — the only regime where every-n theorems for forms were ever proved.
first_step: Construct candidates V_p (e.g. adjoin variables parametrising the Type II h-family or the factorizations of 4Cp+1 into 3 factors) and compute their point counts and singular series.

title: Minimal-counterexample descent: failure at p ⇒ failure at a smaller related prime
connection: Khare–Wintenberger: induction on conductor reduces to base cases. ES: find a map Φ such that if ES (or (★)) fails at p then it fails at some smaller Φ(p) (e.g. a prime factor of 4p+1 or of (p+e)/4); with verification to 10¹⁸ this proves ES.
why: Induction on the size of the counterexample is the cleanest every-n mechanism; data on (★)-failures can test candidate maps directly.
first_step: For the 14 (★)-failing primes, check whether any simple arithmetic function of p (prime factors of 4p+1, 8p+1, (p+3)/4, p−4k², …) systematically produces another (★)-failing prime.

title: Positive proportion of levels with a certificate is false — find the right normalisation
connection: Selberg's positive-proportion step needed the right normalisation (zeros up to height T). For ES at fixed p, only ≍ log²p of ≍ p levels carry certificates; identify the natural finite set of 'attempts' of which a positive proportion succeed (e.g. levels C ≤ (log p)^A, windows e ≤ (log p)^B with weights), so that a positive-proportion statement would be meaningful and imply ES.
why: A positive-proportion statement over a small set of attempts is a pointwise statement; finding the set where proportions are stable is the first step.
first_step: For hard primes, compute success proportions over attempt sets of various shapes and sizes; find shapes where the proportion stays bounded below as p grows.

title: Descent to universal torsors: more variables for the circle method
connection: Heath-Brown and others proved Manin-type results via universal torsors, which have more variables and simpler equations. ES's Type I/II parametrisations (Elsholtz–Tao) look like torsor coordinates; identify the universal torsor of the ES surface (BL computed its Brauer/Picard data) and count integral points on its twists with fixed p.
why: More variables after descent is the standard route to circle-method feasibility; the torsor equations may be quadratic in many variables.
first_step: From BL's description of Pic of the compactification of U_n, write torsor equations and compare with the ET parametrisation n = 4abcd − … ; count variables per equation.
refs: Davenport, Phil. Trans. A 251 (1959)/ Proc. Roy. Soc. A 272 (1963)

title: Drinfeld modular curves X₀(P) point counts as ES solution counters
connection: Type II ES data at P correspond to points on modular-type curves in FF; Drinfeld modular curves have explicit point counts (Gekeler). If the ES count at P equals a Hecke eigenvalue sum, Ramanujan bounds (Drinfeld) give lower bounds.
why: A lower bound from a Ramanujan-type identity is the only FF mechanism that would directly transfer as 'pointwise' information over Z.
first_step: Test numerically in F_3[T] whether #ES-solutions(P) correlates with a_P of some Drinfeld modular form of small level (fit against Gekeler's tables).

title: Spectral world: ES as a statement about eigenvalues of the Laplacian on the triangle orbifold S²(x,y,z)
connection: Area of S²(x,y,z) is 2π(1 − 4/n) for ES triples; Weyl's law relates area to eigenvalue counts, and Selberg trace formula for Δ(x,y,z) involves 1/x, 1/y, 1/z via elliptic terms.
why: Turns the Egyptian equation into a trace-formula identity; spectral rigidity results (isospectrality) could constrain which triples share areas — e.g. how many ES triples exist for given n.
first_step: Low priority; write the elliptic contributions in the trace formula for Δ(x,y,z) and see if 'area = 2π(1 − 4/n)' has a spectral characterization.

title: Feature: finite escalation / certificate threshold (290, 451, Graham's 77)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'finite escalation / certificate threshold (290, 451, Graham's 77)'. ES LACKS (U(n) has sporadic failures to 978145; ES itself has no known threshold theorem). To supply it one could: find a reformulation where an escalation lemma holds: 'if ES-shape S solves all p < B then all p' — unlikely, but record the precise failure
why: Universality theorems for forms are finite-check because of modular-form bounds; ES has no modular generating function.
first_step: Look for a generating series Σ R(n) q^n with modular or mock-modular properties (theta quotients in repo).

title: Tunnell ternary counts as ES predictors
connection: #{x²+2y²+8z² = p} and #{x²+2y²+32z² = p} are weight-3/2 coefficients; their ratio is Tunnell's congruent-number test. Correlate both with k₁, k₂.
why: A weight-3/2 form whose coefficients track ES counts would be the first concrete 'theta lift' fingerprint (Kudla/Shimura direction).
first_step: Brute-force the representation counts for p ≤ 10⁵ (O(p) each with nested loops ≈ fine for p ≤ 2·10⁴).

title: Vieta moves on lifted equations
connection: Introduce an auxiliary variable making an ES constraint quadratic, then examine Vieta root exchange.
why: Lifting may create useful symmetries absent from the original equation, but integrality must be checked.
first_step: Try y+z=s and yz=q, derive the lifted equations, and test root-exchange closures.

title: Spectral gaps of certificate transitions
connection: Construct a finite transition matrix from verified certificate transformations and inspect its bottlenecks.
why: A spectral picture may identify missing moves or separated families, not prove connectivity on its own.
first_step: Enumerate bounded certificates for one p and compute transition components before estimating eigenvalues.

title: Modular energy landscapes
connection: Define an integer energy from violated congruences and exact residual divisibility, with zero energy reserved for checked certificates.
why: The landscape may reveal useful local moves and traps rather than merely a solver score.
first_step: For a bounded parameter box, enumerate energies and locate local minima under unit-coordinate changes.

title: Arithmetic spectral outliers
connection: Associate a finite operator with residue transitions and ask whether spectral outliers align with quadratic-character sectors.
why: A character decomposition can make a spectral pattern arithmetically interpretable.
first_step: Diagonalize a small convolution operator by characters and compare its modes with observed success biases.

title: Finite Fourier uncertainty
connection: Relate concentration of a divisor-residue distribution to concentration of its Fourier transform.
why: A distribution supported on too few residues must carry detectable spectral structure in a finite group.
first_step: Compute support and Fourier support for exact small examples and identify the characters responsible for concentration.

title: Mutation testing for certificate checkers
connection: Deliberately change signs, residues, denominator values, and domain assumptions to test whether a verifier rejects false claims.
why: A checker that accepts corrupted data cannot support trustworthy experiments.
first_step: Create one mutation per required condition and confirm that each is rejected for a mathematical reason.

title: Automorphic periods as counting interpretations
connection: Ask whether an already established lattice or quaternion count can be expressed as a period with arithmetic coefficient meaning.
why: A period formula would connect geometric symmetry to exact counts, but requires a concrete identity rather than analogy alone.
first_step: Write the finite count explicitly and search for an existing period formula matching its group, stabilizer, and congruence level.

title: Quantum unique ergodicity of theta functions and the 'theta quotient' form of ES
connection: Repo mentions a theta-quotient reformulation. QUE for theta functions (Marklof, Lindenstrauss) gives equidistribution of their values; positivity of a specific theta quotient at a specific point is a pointwise question.
why: Theta functions have exact functional equations (rigidity) — a candidate for mechanism (R).
first_step: git grep -il 'theta quotient' -- '*.md' to find the repo's statement; then check whether the quotient is a ratio of Jacobi forms whose Fourier coefficients have a sign-rigidity (e.g. Kronecker–Hurwitz class-number formula).

title: Eichler–Selberg trace formula: Hurwitz class numbers H(4p − t²) sum to traces of Hecke operators — does an ES count hide in a trace?
connection: Σ_t H(4p − t²) = (traces of T_p on cusp forms) + explicit terms (Eichler–Selberg). ES-type counts involve divisors of p² + 4c²d = discriminant-like quantities −(p² + 4c²d) = disc of forms? For Type I, 4c²d + p² ≡ p² mod 4 ≡ 1 mod 4... hmm, −(p² + 4c²d) ≡ 3 mod 4 is a valid negative discriminant! So Type I involves H(p² + 4c²d)-type class numbers summed over c — resembling Σ_t H(4n − t²) with roles of t and n changed (t ↔ p fixed, n ↔ varying c).
why: If Σ_c H(p² + 4c²d) over c in an AP equals a trace of a Hecke operator at p on some space (via a 'reversed' Eichler–Selberg), then positivity/non-vanishing of traces (Deligne bounds give |tr T_p| ≤ (dim)·2p^{(k−1)/2}; not positivity) — more usefully, the trace formula gives an *exact* identity which might convert a 'divisor in class' count into a modular-form coefficient count.
first_step: Search 'Hurwitz class numbers H(p² + 4m) sum' and 'class number sums over quadratic polynomials'; check Eichler–Selberg with weight/level to see if Σ_m H(p² + 4m) (m in an AP) is a known trace.
refs: Zagier, 'Nombres de classes et formes modulaires de poids 3/2'

title: Is f_II(n) (or any ES count) a *multiplicative* or 'quasi-multiplicative' function?
connection: Egyptian-fraction counts are not multiplicative (solutions for pq are not products of solutions for p and q), but there may be a sub-count (e.g. 'primitive' Type II certificates, coprimality-restricted) that is multiplicative or satisfies a Hecke-type relation f(pq) = f(p)f(q) + correction.
why: Multiplicativity would make f a Dirichlet-series coefficient with an Euler product — immediate structure; Hecke-type relations would be modular-form-like.
first_step: Compute f_II(n) for n ≤ 10⁴ and test f(mn) vs f(m)f(n) for coprime m,n; look for a correction term pattern.

title: Rademacher-type exact formula for a mock modular generating function of R(n)
connection: If Σ R(n) q^n (or a twist) were mock modular, Bringmann–Ono-style exact formulas give coefficients as convergent Kloosterman–Bessel series.
why: Exact formulas with positive main term and explicitly bounded tails are how partition-function positivity facts are proved pointwise.
first_step: Check growth: R(n) is polylog, inconsistent with the exponential growth of weight-<0 mock forms; so look for weight-1 or weight-0 objects (logarithmic growth plausible for weight 1 Eisenstein-like). Test whether n ↦ M₀(n) matches a weight-1 Eisenstein coefficient shape.

title: Quantum unique ergodicity analogy: certificates as 'mass' of a p-dependent state
connection: QUE for Hecke eigenforms gives pointwise equidistribution in the eigenvalue aspect ↔ ES certificate counts as 'mass in a small set'.
why: QUE is pointwise in the spectral parameter (Lindenstrauss, Soundararajan); a QUE-type statement for a p-indexed family would give pointwise counts, but the target set must be fixed-size.
first_step: Find whether R(p)/M(p) can be written as ⟨φ_p, 1_A φ_p⟩ for some natural p-family of states φ_p and fixed set A.

title: One-parameter form: R(p) = #{m ≡ 3 (mod 4) : r_p(m) | (m+1)/4}, r_p(m) = (−p mod m) (CHECKED p ≤ 1009)
connection: Trial form (4uC−1) | p+u with m = 4uC−1 forces u = r_p(m) (as 1 ≤ u < m), so R(p) counts moduli m ≡ 3 mod 4 whose ceiling-remainder divides (m+1)/4 ↔ a single-variable search over m.
