why: A one-variable reformulation makes 'remainder of one integer modulo a running modulus' the whole problem — the classical object of the Dirichlet divisor problem and of p mod m statistics (Vinogradov), possibly opening Voronoi/exponential-sum tools.
first_step: Verified numerically (scripts/z52b_free_opus_check1.py, p ≤ 1009 incl. 409 → 0). Next: plot r_p(m)/m against m for hard p and study the arcs where r_p(m) is small (m just above p/q).

title: Tunnell's theta-series criterion for congruent numbers
connection: Tunnell gives a computable ternary quadratic-form criterion for a rational-point question (necessary; sufficient assuming BSD), matching ES's quadratic-form reformulations and theta-series coefficient lens (F19,F31).
why: It is an exact arithmetic criterion whose failure can be tested cheaply, making it a useful model for turning ES into a coefficient-vanishing problem.
first_step: Read Tunnell's theorem statement and compare the two weighted representation counts with the ES theta-quotient coefficient; seek an analogous exact criterion.
refs: J. B. Tunnell, A classical Diophantine problem and modular forms of weight 3/2, Invent. Math. 72 (1983) 323–334

title: Theta series and coefficient nonvanishing
connection: Theta-series problems share F19, F31, F32: arithmetic representations become coefficients of modular generating functions.
why: Coefficient formulas may isolate congruence obstructions or positivity contributions invisible in the original equation.
first_step: Inspect the ES theta-quotient identity and compare it with modular-form coefficient nonvanishing criteria at prime indices.

title: Modular forms and nonvanishing of Fourier coefficients
connection: Coefficient-nonvanishing problems share F19, F20, F36; analytic average nonvanishing may fall short of every prime coefficient.
why: Methods proving nonzero coefficients in specified progressions could give a pointwise route for ES's generating function.
first_step: Identify the modular object, its Eisenstein/cusp decomposition, and available nonvanishing theorems for the relevant prime subsequence.

title: Pilatte two-point log-Chowla improvement via graph spectra
connection: Pilatte (2023) gets (log X)^{−c} savings for two-point log Chowla using spectral bounds for random-like graphs on integers; same graph-on-divisibility template as Helfgott–Radziwiłł.
why: Quantitative spectral inputs are what a fixed-p C-average argument would need.
first_step: Read Pilatte's graph construction and check whether its vertex set can be replaced by an AP {4Cp+1}.
refs: Pilatte, Improved bounds for the two-point logarithmic Chowla conjecture, arXiv:2310.19357

title: Expander mixing on Cayley graphs of (ℤ/e)^× generated by prime factors of N
connection: Alon–Roichman: O(log|G|) random generators give an expander; the ES e-slice uses the Cayley graph on (ℤ/e)^× generated by the ω(N) ≈ log log N prime factors of N.
why: Quantifies precisely why one integer's factors are too few to force −1 (B2) and what extra generators (other slices) would need to be pooled.
first_step: Compute spectral gaps of Cayley graphs of (ℤ/e)^× with generators = prime factors of N and also with pooled generators from several slices sharing e.
refs: Alon–Roichman, Random Cayley graphs and expanders, Random Struct. Alg. 5 (1994)

title: Shifted convolution sums (Blomer, Holowinsky) for Σ_C r(4Cp+1)-type ES sums
connection: Shifted convolution sums Σ a(n)b(n+h) of automorphic coefficients have spectral asymptotics; ES Type I/II correlate divisor-class counts at N and N + (shift) across slices.
why: Second moments of ES counts over C at fixed p are shifted convolutions of Eisenstein coefficients.
first_step: Express Σ_C R_C(p)² as a shifted convolution and compute its main term numerically vs data.
refs: Blomer, Shifted convolution sums and subconvexity bounds for automorphic L-functions, IMRN 2004
Holowinsky, A sieve method for shifted convolution sums, Duke Math. J. 146 (2009)

title: Hecke-like transport between f(n) and f(ℓn)
connection: Solutions for n lift to ℓn (multiplicativity); a Hecke operator T_ℓ on solution sets would also need an adjoint pulling solutions from ℓn back to n, which is exactly the missing direction for primes.
why: If solution counts satisfied Hecke-type relations (f(ℓ²n) related to f(n), f(ℓn)), one could deduce f(p) > 0 from composite data.
first_step: Compute f(n), f(ℓn), f(ℓ²n) for n prime ≤ 10^5, ℓ ≤ 13 and fit linear relations; check whether any Hecke-type identity holds.

title: OAI 178 deterministic nonbipartite Ramanujan graphs (claimed) — explicit expanders for ES search
connection: OAI 178 claims deterministic constructions of Ramanujan graphs of all fixed degrees; explicit expanders give derandomised search/sampling over large certificate spaces.
why: Computational: deterministic sampling of (C,d) certificate grids with guaranteed coverage could make adversarial ES searches (DISPROOF_AVENUES) more efficient.
first_step: Check whether an expander walk over C ∈ [1, X] gives better coverage of ES certificates per factoring call than linear scan on hard primes.

title: Murmurations for ES counts (He–Lee–Oliver–Pozdnyakov; Zubrilina)
connection: Murmurations: averages of Frobenius traces a_p over families ordered by conductor show oscillations in p/N, explained by Zubrilina via trace formula; ES counts f(p) averaged over p in a window with normalisation by a scale (e.g. 4C ~ p^θ) might show analogous oscillations.
why: A murmuration-type oscillation would reveal a hidden spectral term in ES counts — new structure for heuristics.
first_step: Plot normalised ES counts f(p)/log²p averaged over p in windows against p mod M / p modulo small structures and against p/X for X ranges; look for oscillatory patterns.
refs: He–Lee–Oliver–Pozdnyakov, Murmurations of elliptic curves, arXiv:2204.10140

title: Nicolas–Serre Hecke algebra mod 2 for parity of ES counts
connection: Nicolas–Serre describe coefficients of modular forms mod 2 via a nilpotent Hecke algebra; the repo PROVED complement pairing makes level counts even and R(p)/2 mod 2 looks like a fair coin.
why: If ES counts relate to Eisenstein coefficients, their parities might be governed by mod-2 modular forms rather than randomness.
first_step: Compute R(p)/2 mod 2 and the parity of class-divisor counts at 4Cp+1 and compare with the mod-2 behaviour of the corresponding Eisenstein coefficients.
refs: Nicolas–Serre, Formes modulaires de niveau 1 en caractéristique 2…, C. R. Math. 350 (2012)

title: Radchenko–Viazovska Fourier interpolation applied to ES lattice theta data (speculative)
connection: Fourier interpolation reconstructs f from values at √n and f̂ at √n; ES lattice reformulations have theta series whose coefficients count certificates.
why: Interpolation formulas give exact identities linking counts at different scales — potentially forcing a nonzero coefficient.
first_step: Check whether ES certificate counts are coefficients of a theta series of a fixed-dimension lattice; if not, close.
refs: Radchenko–Viazovska, Fourier interpolation on the real line, Publ. IHES 129 (2019), arXiv:1701.00265

title: Bruinier–Funke theta lifts / Borcherds products for ES generating functions
connection: Theta lifts produce modular generating functions of traces/cycle counts; Borcherds products give automorphic forms with prescribed divisors. ES counts across p could be coefficients of such a lift if they are traces over class groups.
why: A Borcherds-type product with zeros encoding ES failures would turn ES into a divisor statement for an automorphic form.
first_step: Test whether Σ_p f(p) q^p (or a class-group-trace version) is the holomorphic part of a weak harmonic Maass form by checking coefficient growth and congruences.
refs: Bruinier–Funke, On two geometric theta lifts, Duke Math. J. 125 (2004)

title: Theta quotient / eta-quotient identities for ES counts (exact formulas)
connection: Eta-quotient identities give exact divisor-sum formulas for representation numbers (e.g. r₄, r₈); ES has theta-quotient reformulations in the repo.
why: An exact formula (sum of divisor functions) for some ES-adjacent count would make positivity checkable.
first_step: Search the ES theta-quotient reformulation for a modular form of small level whose coefficients equal an ES sub-count; test by computing 200 coefficients.
refs: Köhler, Eta Products and Theta Series Identities (2011)

title: Expander walk sampling + Ramanujan graphs for Monte Carlo estimates of M_BM constants
connection: Expander-walk Chernoff bounds give sharp concentration for Monte Carlo with few random bits; estimating Euler-product-type constants and certificate densities by sampling primes benefits.
why: Minor computational gain; listed as a concrete use of Ramanujan-graph technology.
first_step: Implement expander-walk sampling of primes in [X, 2X] and compare variance of estimates of mean f(p) with i.i.d. sampling.
refs: Gillman, A Chernoff bound for random walks on expander graphs, SIAM J. Comput. 27 (1998)

title: Hecke operators on the space of words: does T_ℓ map ES₅ words of p to words of ℓp or ℓ²p?
connection: Hecke operators act on SL₂(ℤ)-cosets/matrices with fixed determinant structure. Words are SL₂ matrices with upper-right entry p. Hecke correspondences relate matrices with entry p to entry ℓp.
why: It is the modular-forms-native way to get relations between different n. A Hecke-equivariant structure on certificates would allow induction.
first_step: Apply the coset representatives of T_2 to γ_w and check which images are words (positive, upper-right p or 4p) and how the sign transforms.

title: Brandt matrices: theta series of ternary lattices of maximal orders and the representation number of certificates
connection: Brandt matrix entries are representation numbers of the norm forms of ideals in B_{p,∞}; their traces relate to class numbers of imaginary quadratic orders (Eichler trace formula). Certificate counts at level d may be Brandt-matrix entries.
why: Eichler's trace formula is an exact class-number identity. If certificate counts are traces, they become class-number sums, and class numbers are positive.
first_step: Compute Brandt matrices B(m) for p < 200 (Sage/Magma) and correlate entries with ES level counts.
refs: Gross, Heights and special values of L-series (1987) §§1–2

title: Waldspurger/Kohnen–Zagier: squares of half-integral-weight coefficients as central L-values
connection: SIGN_IDENTITY Prop 2.4 restricts the Waldspurger route. In native terms: if the ES count (or its sign part) were |c(p)|² for a weight-3/2 form, nonvanishing would be L(f⊗χ_p, 1/2) ≠ 0, which is known for positive proportions (Iwaniec–Sarnak type) but not pointwise.
why: Calibration: shows the best automorphic route yields positive proportion, unless a root-number obstruction is absent and an exact formula exists.
first_step: Record calibration; check whether any weight-3/2 form's coefficients correlate with N₋(p) on p < 10⁵ (it should be ruled out by size).

title: Shimura curve / quaternion Shimura lift of the ES theta series
connection: The theta multiplier sign (bsB_theta_multiplier) is weight-1/2 data. The Shimura correspondence maps half-integral to integral weight. ES's sign function on certificate matrices might lift to a function on a Shimura curve's CM points.
why: It would place the sign inside an automorphic representation where nonvanishing theory exists. Zero-propagation was refuted (O175), so only the lifting is new.
first_step: Look at O175 notes (bsB_theta_multiplier) and identify which level and character a 'certificate theta series' would have; compute the first 50 coefficients.

title: Borcherds products / divisors of automorphic forms with zeros at CM points
connection: A Borcherds product has explicit divisor supported on Heegner/CM points. If ES failure at p corresponded to a CM point where some form must vanish, the Borcherds lift might prohibit it.
why: It is the native 'existence via zeros of modular functions' tool, with exact divisor formulas. Speculative but categorically meaningful.
first_step: Read BRAINSTORM/bsC_valence_borcherds.md for the prior attempt; identify which weakly holomorphic input (principal part) would encode certificate data.
refs: Borcherds, Automorphic forms with singularities on Grassmannians (Invent. 1998)

title: Dedekind eta multiplier and the ES sign: (A/p) as an eta-multiplier value on γ_w
connection: The eta multiplier ε(γ) is given by Dedekind sums, and Rademacher's formulas relate it to Jacobi symbols. The ES sign is the theta multiplier on γ_w (bsB_theta_multiplier), and θ and η multipliers are related (θ = η⁵/(η²η²)-type identities).
why: Expressing the sign via η multipliers gives a conjugacy-invariant (Rademacher Φ function / class invariant), which might be easier to sum over words.
first_step: Compute Rademacher's Φ(γ_w) (and separately the Rademacher symbol) for words at p < 1000 and check whether either, mod 8 or 24, determines the sign.

title: Waldspurger-type formula: is some ES deviation a central L-value?
connection: Ono–Soundararajan proved Ramanujan's form under GRH because coefficient² ∝ L(1/2, f⊗χ_n) (Waldspurger), which GRH bounds. ES: look for an ES generating function with a cuspidal component whose p-th coefficient² is a twisted central value.
why: If such a formula existed, GRH (or subconvexity) would bound the deviation pointwise; METAPLECTIC says level series are Eisenstein + theta quotients, so a cusp form would have to come from a different construction (e.g. products/derivatives).
first_step: Decompose products of two level series (or the all-level series) into Eisenstein + cuspidal parts at small level numerically (Sage modular symbols) and look for nonzero cuspidal components.

title: Hecke-type relations between ES counts at p, pℓ, pℓ² (Soundararajan's no-escape-of-mass)
connection: Soundararajan prevented escape of mass using λ(ℓ)² = λ(ℓ²) + 1, which forbids both λ(ℓ) and λ(ℓ²) small. ES: find exact or approximate relations between certificate counts f(p), f(pℓ), f(pℓ²) (solutions for composite n come from p, from ℓ, and 'mixed') that make f(p) = 0 incompatible with the controlled values at pℓ, pℓ².
why: Multiplicative relations at related integers are a way to get pointwise information from quantities that are easier to bound.
first_step: Compute f_II(n) (or R(n)) for n = p, pℓ, pℓ² for p ≤ 10⁵, ℓ ≤ 50, and fit f(pℓ) ≈ a·f(p) + b·f(ℓ) + c·f(p)f(ℓ) + mixed; study the mixed term.

title: Classify limit measures of normalised certificate data along hypothetical failing sequences
connection: QE (density one) comes from a variance bound; QUE (every) from classifying all possible limits (measure rigidity + entropy). ES: attach to each p a normalised measure (levels/shapes of certificates or profinite residue data); show that the only possible limit along any sequence p_k → ∞ is the 'Haar' one, incompatible with R(p_k) = 0.
why: Shifts from 'bound the variance' (almost all) to 'classify limits' (every) — the exact conceptual step of QUE.
first_step: Define μ_p on the profinite completion (or on (ℤ/M)* for growing M) from the residues of p; check what the square-mimicking points of B1 look like as limit measures.

title: Positive entropy from arithmetic recurrence on certificate shapes
connection: Bourgain–Lindenstrauss: Hecke recurrence forces positive entropy, ruling out concentration on small sets. ES: Hecke-like correspondences on certificate shapes (if they exist, cf. LINNIK-ERG item) would force any limiting distribution of shapes to be spread, hence to charge every region with positive mass.
why: Speculative but it is the precise ingredient that made QUE every-form.
first_step: First establish a correspondence (see Hecke-operator item); then measure numerically the entropy of the shape distribution of (★) solutions as p grows.

title: Modular forms mod ℓ for the ES word series
connection: Ono used half-integral weight forms mod m and Serre's Hecke-nilpotence/Chebotarev results to get congruences for every prime modulus. Reduce the ES word series W(q) = Σ_{t,u,v≥2} q^{tuv−u−v} (or the level series of Thm K) mod 2 or 3 and look for congruences with eta/theta quotients that determine R(p) mod m from p's class.
why: A modular congruence 'R(p) ≡ nonzero (mod m) on a class' is an every-p statement on that class.
first_step: Compute W(q) mod 2, mod 3 to 10⁶ terms and test linear relations with products of θ(q^k), η(q^k) modulo 2/3.
refs: Ono, Ann. Math. 151 (2000) 293-307 (Distribution of the partition function modulo m)

title: Dual certificates: an exact 'magic function' proving positivity of a weighted ES count
connection: Viazovska's proof found an exact auxiliary function (from modular forms) satisfying sign conditions — a dual certificate. ES: seek weights w on certificate shapes and an exact identity Σ w·(certificates of p) = (explicit positive function of p) + (manifestly nonnegative terms), with the identity coming from modular forms (Thm K level series).
why: Positivity via an exact identity with sign conditions is a way to bypass error terms entirely.
first_step: Using the Thm K series, search linear combinations of level series (with q-expansion coefficients) whose p-th coefficient is a nonnegative combination of R_t(p) plus a known positive term.
refs: arXiv:1603.04246 (Viazovska, The sphere packing problem in dimension 8)

title: Escape of mass for ES: certificates drifting to extreme shapes
connection: Soundararajan's step was 'no escape of mass': limiting measures are probability measures. ES analogue: as p → ∞, could the certificates' normalized shape distribution (log C / log p, log u / log p) concentrate at the boundary (C ≈ 1 or C ≈ p), so that 'typical' regions are empty? Show mass stays in the bulk.
why: If certificates escape to extreme shapes for hard p, proofs focusing on bulk shapes miss them; if not, bulk counting suffices.
first_step: For hard primes vs controls, compute the empirical distribution of (log C/log p, log u/log p) of all certificates.

title: Modularity of an ES generating object and a 'level-lowering' contradiction
connection: Ribet's level lowering forced a hypothetical form to level 2 where none exists. ES generating functions (Thm K level series) are modular of level t; a failure of ES at p might force some auxiliary modular form (e.g. a twisted combination vanishing at p) to have a special property that lowers its level or weight to a space that is empty.
why: Speculative, but 'empty space of modular forms' contradictions are the archetypal every-n mechanism.
first_step: Search for linear combinations of level-t series whose p-th coefficient is R(p) times a nonzero constant, and determine the space they live in; ask whether vanishing at all ES-failing p would force membership in a smaller space.

title: Fourier interpolation/uniqueness: ES data at primes determine a function vanishing somewhere?
connection: Radchenko–Viazovska Fourier interpolation shows a function is determined by values at √n. Odd idea: the function n ↦ R(n) (or its smoothed version) is determined by data on a sparse set via modular identities (Thm K); if R vanished at p, interpolation formulas would force a contradiction with positivity elsewhere.
why: Interpolation/uniqueness theorems from modular forms are a way to transfer information between sparse and dense sets of n.
first_step: Check whether Thm K level series admit Rademacher/Fourier-interpolation-type formulas expressing R(p) via values at other n with explicit kernels.
refs: arXiv:1603.04246 (Viazovska, The sphere packing problem in dimension 8)

title: Hecke operators on ES counts as functions of n: R(nℓ) vs R(n) for split/inert ℓ
connection: QUE uses Hecke operators T_ℓ acting on eigenfunctions. Define T_ℓ on functions of n by (T_ℓ f)(n) = f(nℓ) + (character)·f(n/ℓ) and test whether R (or f_II) is approximately an eigenfunction of some T_ℓ on Mordell-hard n, with eigenvalue depending on (n/ℓ).
why: An approximate Hecke structure would give the multiplicative relations needed for Soundararajan-type arguments.
first_step: Regress f_II(nℓ) on f_II(n) for n prime and ℓ ≤ 50, separately for (n/ℓ) = ±1.

title: Moments in the level aspect at fixed p: Σ_C |D_C(p) − E_C|² via spectral methods
connection: Subconvexity proofs bound moments of families by spectral decomposition. At fixed p, the family of levels C gives the moment Σ_{C ≤ X} |D_C(p) − E_C|²; express it via sums of Kloosterman sums (Kuznetsov) and bound it pointwise in p.
why: A good level-aspect second moment at fixed p would show the deviations are small for most levels — then a positive proportion of levels with expected positive counts carry certificates.
first_step: Compute the moment numerically for p ~ 10⁸ and compare with Σ E_C (if Var ≈ mean, the moment is Poisson-like).

title: Uniform spectral gap for the 'ES move graph' on residues mod q
connection: Bourgain–Gamburd give uniform expansion of Cayley graphs mod q. Define a graph on (ℤ/q)³ (or on SL₂(ℤ/q)) by ES-preserving moves (change of one word parameter) and test for a uniform spectral gap in q; uniform mixing would give quantitative equidistribution of words mod q with archimedean size control.
why: Uniform-in-q expansion is the input for affine-sieve/Bourgain–Kontorovich-type counting, which is how thin-orbit local-global results are proved.
first_step: Compute the spectral gap of the move graph for primes q ≤ 200 and look for uniformity.

title: Rectangle tilings: ES ⇔ an n×4 rectangle split into three horizontal strips, each a row of equal squares
connection: A strip of width W tiled by x equal squares has height W/x; three strips stacked give height W(1/x+1/y+1/z). Thus ES(n) ⇔ the rectangle of aspect n : 4 is tiled by three such strips.
why: Tiling theory (Dehn's theorem, Laczkovich–Szekeres tilings with similar rectangles) studies which aspect ratios are tileable under constraints; ES is a 3-strip constrained tiling.
first_step: Formalize and check whether allowing strips to be split further (two-level tilings) yields a known Dehn-type characterization that ES is a restriction of.

title: Transfer: Kneser/Olson subset-product theory for gate G4
connection: Stewart's criterion: a fraction fails 2-term representation iff the prime factors of the relevant integer lie in a subgroup H avoiding −1. Kneser/Olson/Davenport-constant bounds describe when subset products must hit −1.
why: ES failure ⟺ for every C, all prime factors of the relevant auxiliary integers lie in subgroups H_C ∌ −1 — a simultaneous confinement over many C.
first_step: Quantify: for random integers N ≡ 1 mod q, the probability of H-confinement ≈ (log N)^{−(1−1/[G:H])}; multiply over independent C to get the heuristic failure rate; compare with data.

title: Connection: sum-product phenomena mod q for 'p ≡ −e mod 4ab, e | a+b'
connection: Type II couples a product (4ab) with a sum (a+b) through divisibility; sum-product estimates force mixed sets to cover residues, but the problem's residue question is trivial locally — the content is integrality and size.
why: Records that sum-product tools address local covering (already free for ES) — a dividing-line non-feature.
first_step: None; note only.

title: Feature: character-sorted family covering — ES as a covering of the 'character cube' {±1}^ℓ
connection: Group certificate families by the quadratic-character pattern they require. ES then needs: for every pattern realised by a prime p (all patterns except 'all +1' for squares), some family compatible with that pattern also hits p's finer class. The coarse layer is a covering of the Boolean cube minus the all-ones corner.
why: Makes T1 (all-ones corner uncovered) and ES (every other corner eventually covered) two parts of one combinatorial statement; the coarse layer may be provable by finite combinatorics.
first_step: Compute, for ℓ ≤ 7 small primes, which corners of {±1}^ℓ are covered by at least one family with s ≤ 1000 (coarse layer), and how the fine layer behaves inside each corner.

title: Hard primes are p ≡ 1 mod a large smooth modulus — compare with Carmichael/Korselt primes
connection: 2521, 1201, 3361, 20521, 21841, 4201, 14401, 9601 all have p−1 divisible by 2⁴·3·5² or 2⁴·3·5·7 etc.; these are exactly the primes used to build Carmichael numbers (Erdős construction, p−1 | L).
why: Shared extremal structure (p−1 | L for smooth L) — tools for counting such primes (AGP, Erdős) could count ES-hard candidates.
first_step: Test: are ES-hard primes over-represented among prime factors of Carmichael numbers ≤ 10¹²? (Pinch's tables).

title: 'lcm-closed' solutions (x | z): fail only at 2521 among all primes ≤ 10⁵ and all n ≤ 3000
connection: Solutions with x | z (equivalently y | z in the data: identical failure set and share 0.377) exist for every prime ≤ 10⁵ except 2521 = lcm(1..10)+1, the hardest ES prime; none of the 9 solutions of 4/2521 has x | z.
why: A sub-family with a single exception ≤ 10⁵ — and the exception is the extremal 'all small primes split' prime. 4/p = (a + b + 1)/z with a, b | z is a pure 'three divisors of z summing to 4z/p' problem: a practical-number style formulation.
first_step: Extend to 10⁷; test whether failures are exactly primes ≡ 1 (mod lcm(1..k)) with k large; prove x | z ⟺ y | z for prime n.

title: Partition function parity p(p) mod 2 vs ES counts (null test)
connection: Brief asks for partition-type comparisons: compute p(n) mod 2 and mod 3 for n ≤ 2·10⁵ (Euler pentagonal recurrence) and correlate with residual U at primes.
why: Expected null (no known link); a positive result would be a genuine surprise linking ES to modular forms of weight −1/2.
first_step: Implement the pentagonal recurrence mod 2/3 in numpy and run the Spearman test.

title: Divisor posets
connection: Organize divisors of each p-tied integer by divisibility and study where the target residue first occurs.
why: Poset structure may reveal that a few prime-factor toggles suffice to reach the target.
first_step: Construct divisor Hasse diagrams for 20 auxiliary integers and color nodes by target residues.

title: Subset products in residue groups
connection: Translate selection of a divisor into selecting prime-power factors whose product hits a residue in a finite multiplicative group.
why: This gives an exact finite combinatorial problem once the factorization is known.
first_step: For a factored auxiliary integer, run subset-product dynamic programming and inspect unreachable residue classes.

title: Zero-sum theory for divisor residues
connection: Take discrete-log coordinates when available and compare target divisor residues with zero-sum sequence phenomena.
why: Multiplicative divisor selection becomes additive combinatorics in finite abelian groups.
first_step: For cyclic unit groups of small moduli, compute the exponent multiset and shortest subsequences hitting the target.

title: Prime divisors in prescribed classes
connection: Study which prime-factor residue patterns of 4Cp+1 are sufficient to produce a target divisor.
why: Some successes may follow from one or two factors rather than the whole divisor set.
first_step: Enumerate minimal sufficient factor-residue multisets for small moduli.

title: Additive energy of log-residue sets
connection: In a cyclic residue group, take discrete logs of available factor residues and measure additive energy.
why: High energy signals a structured subset-product obstruction that can be described concretely.
first_step: Compute sumset sizes and energies for factor-log sets at moduli with cyclic unit group.

title: Sum–product mixing across parameters
connection: Compare multiplicative divisor generation with additive changes in the auxiliary parameter.
why: Alternating two different operations may escape concentration that persists under either alone.
first_step: Build a small state graph with factor multiplication and valid parameter-shift edges, checking each edge algebraically.

title: Witness hypergraphs
connection: Build a hypergraph whose vertices are auxiliary choices and whose edges are jointly compatible pieces of a certificate.
why: Compatibility may be more naturally expressed by small tuples than by one successful parameter.
first_step: For one exact parametrization, separate its constraints into three pieces and enumerate compatible triples for a small prime.

title: Determinantal matching encodings
connection: Ask whether a restricted certificate family can be encoded as perfect matchings with a nonvanishing determinant witness.
why: A matching formulation could import exact combinatorial certificates, but the encoding must avoid spurious solutions.
first_step: Construct a bipartite compatibility graph for a toy factor-allocation problem and test which matchings yield ES triples.

title: Matroids for family diversity
connection: Treat residue tests supplied by candidate families as feature vectors and use independence to choose a diverse search portfolio.
why: Linear independence is a cheap surrogate for avoiding many near-identical families.
first_step: Build a binary family-by-test matrix on small primes and compare independent subsets with greedy coverage subsets.

title: Transversal numbers of failure patterns
connection: Represent each observed failure pattern by the families that repair it and study the minimum hitting set.
why: This extracts complementary mechanisms rather than just ranking individually successful identities.
first_step: Compute a minimum hitting set for a bounded family-prime incidence matrix.

title: Ramsey extraction of parameter patterns
connection: Color small parameter tuples by which certificate mechanism succeeds and look for structured monochromatic configurations.
why: Regular patterns can suggest identities, provided each conjectured identity is checked algebraically.
first_step: Color a bounded parameter grid and search for rectangles whose four corners share a symbolic template.

title: Arithmetic progressions inside witness sets
connection: Look for long arithmetic progressions of successful auxiliary parameters and derive the conditions responsible.
why: Progressions may signal a hidden congruence family rather than random abundance.
first_step: For fixed small primes, find maximal progressions of successful C and compare their differences with the factorization of p−1.

title: Combinatorial word lines
connection: Encode elementary matrix choices as words and ask whether varying one wildcard block preserves an ES-relevant identity.
why: A combinatorial line could package many related certificates into a single construction.
first_step: Enumerate short matrix words with one repeated wildcard and symbolically compute their coordinate expressions.

title: Residue graph homomorphisms
connection: Map an integral certificate-transition graph to its reductions modulo several small integers.
why: Fibers and missing lifts can reveal exactly what information a residue graph forgets.
first_step: Construct the reduction map for a bounded transition graph and inspect fibers of successful residue states.

title: Partitions of the reciprocal mass
connection: Connect ES to restricted partition problems after multiplying by a common denominator L: 4L/p=L/x+L/y+L/z.
why: The summands are divisors of L, so this is an exact three-part divisor partition when p divides L.
first_step: For several small multiples L of p, enumerate three-divisor partitions of 4L/p.

title: Matrix-tree determinants
connection: Compare determinant expressions from the forest formulation with graph Laplacian cofactors.
why: A graph realization could make positivity or combinatorial multiplicity transparent.
first_step: Construct small weighted trees and check which Laplacian minors reproduce short tuv−u−v expressions.

title: Sandpile groups as residue containers
connection: Investigate whether cokernels of Laplacians appearing in certificate encodings organize denominator congruences.
why: The finite abelian group retains integral information beyond a real determinant.
first_step: For a candidate graph encoding, compute its Smith normal form and compare invariant factors with certificate moduli.

title: Nonbacktracking certificate walks
connection: Forbid immediate inverse moves in a certificate graph and compare the resulting exploration with unrestricted walks.
why: Avoiding trivial reversals may expose genuine cycles and increase search diversity.
first_step: Enumerate nonbacktracking paths of length at most eight in a small verified transition graph.

title: Graph covers and congruence refinement
connection: View reduction modulo a larger modulus as a refinement of a smaller residue-state graph.
why: Covering-like behavior could make iterative modular analysis systematic; exceptional fibers are equally informative.
first_step: Compare transition graphs modulo 4 and 8 and classify how vertices and edges lift.

title: Random spanning-tree exploration
connection: Sample spanning trees of a finite certificate graph to obtain nonredundant exploration routes.
why: The tree removes cycles while retaining reachability within the sampled component.
first_step: Compare the distinct parameter regions visited by depth-first search and random-tree-guided search under equal budgets.

title: Tilings that encode reciprocal sums
connection: Represent unit fractions as areas of equal-height rectangles after choosing a common grid.
why: A carefully constrained tiling model may turn divisibility and positivity into visible local conditions.
first_step: For a fixed L divisible by p, draw three rectangles of areas L/x,L/y,L/z summing to 4L/p and record grid restrictions.

title: Cavity messages on factor graphs
connection: Represent local valuation and congruence constraints as a factor graph and pass approximate marginal messages.
why: Belief propagation can suggest assignments, while exact substitution verifies every output.
first_step: Build a small factor graph for residue-factor selection and compare message marginals with exhaustive enumeration.

title: Tensor-network contraction of residue constraints
connection: Represent factor choices and congruence checks as small tensors and contract along a low-width graph.
why: Contraction order can exploit sparse dependencies in exact witness counting.
first_step: Construct a residue-selection tensor network for at most ten factors and compare contraction widths.

title: Holographic changes of basis
connection: Test whether a basis change simplifies local tensors in a finite certificate constraint network.
why: Some encodings become easier after transforming the local representation, but all arithmetic constraints must survive.
first_step: Apply small invertible basis changes to a toy residue tensor and compare sparsity and contraction cost.

title: Equality saturation for rational identities
connection: Store equivalent rational expressions in an e-graph and extract forms with simpler integrality conditions.
why: Equivalent formulas can have very different arithmetic usability even when their real values agree.
first_step: Build an e-graph from a few verified reciprocal identities and score expressions by denominator-factor complexity.

title: Treewidth of arithmetic factor graphs
connection: Measure the width of a factor graph after separating valuations, carries, and residues.
why: Small treewidth would support exact dynamic programming for that bounded encoding.
first_step: Construct three alternative factor graphs for the same tiny instance and compare elimination widths.

title: Decision diagrams for factor subsets
connection: Compress repeated residual subproblems using zero-suppressed decision diagrams or related shared DAGs.
why: Many distinct divisors can share the same remaining residue problem.
first_step: Build a small decision diagram for target-residue divisor selection and compare its node count with the number of divisors.

title: Approximate common divisors as hints
connection: Explore cases where several auxiliary values are near multiples of an unknown useful factor.
why: Shared approximate divisibility might reveal a factor-selection strategy if the error model is justified.
first_step: Construct exact small examples from known certificates and test whether the useful factor is recoverable from the proposed hints.

title: Partial factor bits from congruence constraints
connection: Use the required residue of a useful divisor as partial information in a factorization problem.
why: A residue class supplies genuine bits of structure, though it may be far too weak for existing algorithms.
first_step: For small auxiliary integers, measure how much the target congruence shrinks the divisor search and check partial-factor recovery literature.

title: Factor-graph neural heuristics
connection: Use a graph model whose nodes represent prime factors, residues, and valuation slots to rank partial assignments.
why: The architecture mirrors actual arithmetic constraints, while final outputs still require exact verification.
first_step: Train only on tiny exhaustively solved factor-selection instances and test ranking quality on larger held-out ones.

title: Motifs in proof graphs
connection: Mine repeated small subgraphs in graphs of exact algebraic derivations.
why: Recurring proof fragments may become reusable lemmas or identity-generation macros.
first_step: Encode ten elementary derivations as operation DAGs and identify repeated three-operation motifs.

title: Citation-graph bridges
connection: Trace papers that connect two relevant areas, such as restricted divisor problems and finite-group zero-sum theory.
why: Bridge papers may supply a transferable lemma not indexed under Egyptian fractions.
first_step: Search for a paper using both topic vocabularies, verify it exists, and inspect its cited technical tools.

title: Ising model on the modular-hyperbola graph of N
connection: The modular hyperbola xy ≡ −1 (mod e) restricted to divisors of N ↔ an Ising/Potts model whose ground-state energy is 0 iff the e-slice is non-empty.
why: Ground-state problems on frustrated graphs are where spin-glass theory produces sharp phase diagrams; ES asks for 'no frustration' at every p.
first_step: Build the graph (vertices = divisors of N, edges = pairs with ab⁻¹ ≡ −1 mod e) for a few hundred p, compute frustration index vs log p, look for a universal scaling law.

title: Pólya's 'random walk on divisors' and first-passage to the class −1 mod 4C
connection: Model the multiplicative group (ℤ/4C)^× as a Cayley graph generated by the prime factors of 4Cp+1; the subset-product set is the set reachable in ≤ ω steps; ES(p) asks that for some C the walk reaches −1.
why: Reachability in Cayley graphs with few generators is studied in expander/diameter theory (Babai conjecture, Helfgott); diameters of abelian Cayley graphs are explicit.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵, compute for each C ≤ 100 the subgroup generated by prime factors of 4Cp+1 mod 4C and whether −1 lies in it; separate 'subgroup misses −1' from 'subgroup contains −1 but subset-product misses'.

title: Dimer / Kasteleyn determinant count of e-slice solutions
connection: Solutions on an e-slice are pairs (a,b) with ab | N and ab⁻¹ ≡ −1 (mod e); this is a perfect-matching-like count in a bipartite graph (a's vs b's) and Kasteleyn's method computes matching counts as Pfaffians.
why: Pfaffian expressions give exact, sometimes positive formulas (e.g. Aztec diamond), unlike sieve bounds.
first_step: Construct the bipartite graph for a few N and check planarity (likely not), then check whether the count has a determinant formula anyway via the group structure (it's a convolution over (ℤ/e)^×).

title: Spectral gap of the 'ES Laplacian' on the forest reformulation
connection: Repo mentions a forest reformulation. Forests have Laplacians; Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem counts spanning forests as determinants. Ask whether f(p) (or an e-slice count) is a determinant/minor of a p-dependent Laplacian.
why: Determinant formulas are exact and sometimes provably nonzero by congruence/sign arguments.
first_step: git grep -il forest -- '*.md' to find the repo's reformulation; test whether the count equals a Laplacian minor for p ≤ 100.

title: Hidden-shift/period structure in the e-slice subset-product sets
connection: The set S_N(e) = {ab⁻¹ mod e : ab | N} is a 'sumset' in log coordinates; Freiman/Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers structure theorems describe sets with small doubling, and the group-theoretic Kneser theorem gives |S + S| bounds. ES needs −1 ∈ S for some e.
why: Additive-combinatorics structure of S_N could show S_N(e) is 'almost a subgroup' for many e — then membership of −1 is a character-sum question.
first_step: Compute |S_N(e)| and |S·S| relative to e for p ≤ 10⁵ and all admissible e ≤ 4p; look for e where S is a near-subgroup.

title: Ramsey-type unavoidable patterns: among any K consecutive primes ≡ 1 mod 24, must one have a solution with C ≤ 2?
connection: Even if not every prime has a small-C solution, maybe 'small-C solvability' has bounded gaps along primes (van der Waerden-ish). Not ES itself but a sub-statement with a combinatorial flavour.
why: Bounded-gap statements can be proved by covering + pigeonhole; data shows which K is plausible.
first_step: Compute the longest run of consecutive primes ≡ 1 mod 24 up to 10⁸ with no C ≤ 2 (resp. ≤ 5, ≤ 10) solution.

title: Is 'no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C' equivalent to 'all prime factors lie in a −1-free subgroup' when the subset-product set is a subgroup? (structure lemma)
connection: Subset products of the prime factors of N generate a submonoid of (ℤ/4C)^×; since the group is finite, the submonoid is a subgroup H; −1 ∉ H iff N's factors generate a −1-free subgroup. So 'C fails for p' ⟺ the prime factors of 4Cp+1 generate a subgroup of (ℤ/4C)^× not containing −1 — IF the subset-product set (with multiplicities) equals the generated subgroup, which needs enough multiplicity. With multiplicity-1 factors it's only the 'subset products', a subset of H.
why: Clarifying exactly when 'generated subgroup' = 'subset product set' (gate G4 in the repo) matters: if the gap is empirically negligible, the failure condition is a clean Galois condition (all factors split in a certain abelian extension), i.e. ES ⟺ 'for some C, 4Cp+1 has a prime factor inert in a subfield' — a Chebotarev-at-a-point shape.

title: Monks–Moore style 'hypergraph' of Egyptian-fraction decompositions and Hall's marriage theorem
connection: Hall's theorem gives existence of systems of distinct representatives from counting conditions; for the family of sets S_C = {divisors of 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C}, ES needs ONE non-empty set, not an SDR — a much weaker requirement. But Hall-type 'defect' versions (König) give lower bounds on how many sets are non-empty from global counts.
why: Trivial direction: Σ_C |S_C| ≥ 1 ⟹ some S_C ≠ ∅; the campaign's M_BM is exactly the average of Σ_C |S_C| over p. The marriage-theorem lens asks instead for *structural* reasons (a bipartite graph between C's and divisor classes with a perfect matching for all p) — equivalent to a 'universal' witness assignment.
